heading: OWASP Top 10
text: (Open Web Application Security Project OR Open Worldwide Application Security Project) What is DevSecOps? It refers to the integration of security practices into a DevOps software delivery model. It is the practice of integrating security into every phase of the software development lifecycle (SDLC) instead of treating it as a final gate before release. In a DevSecOps model, security objectives are integrated as early as possible in the lifecycle of software development and security considerations are important throughout the lifecycle. Vulnerabilities A security vulnerability is a software code flaw or a system misconfiguration that hackers can use to gain unauthorized access to a system or network. A vulnerability is a weakness in software, configuration, or process that an attacker can exploit to compromise confidentiality, integrity, or availability (the CIA triad). Exploit An exploit is the method hackers used to exploit a vulnerability and exploit is typically a piece of custom software or a sequence of commands. Threat A threat is the actual or hypothetical event in which one or more exploits vulnerability to mount an attack. Key terminology 	 Term Definition - - Vulnerability A weakness (e.g., unsanitized input) Threat Something that could exploit a weakness (attacker, malware) Exploit Code or technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability. Risk Likelihood x impact of a threat exploiting a vulnerability. Attack Surface Sum of all points where an attacker can interact with the system (APIs, forms, ports, dependencies). Payload The malicious data sent during an attack. Zero-day A vulnerability with no available patch, often unknown to the vendor. PoC Proof of Concept: demonstrates that a vulnerability is exploitable. What is DevOps? A set of practices that combines software development and IT Operations. It aims to shorten the Systems Development Lifecycle and provides continuous delivery with high software availability. DevOps vs DevSecOps Aspect DevOps DevSecOps - - - Goal Deliver software faster and more reliably Deliver software faster, reliably, and securely Security Timing Often a late-stage review/gate Continuous, from planning onward Ownership Dev + Ops Dev + Sec + Ops Pipeline Build -> Test -> Deploy Build -> Security scans -> Test -> Policy checks -> Deploy -> Runtime monitoring Cost of fixing bugs Security bugs found late are expensive Found early, cheap to fix Culture Collaboration between dev and ops Collaboration between dev, ops and security Compliance Manual audits Automated, continuous compliance checks Feedback Loop Test failures Test failures plus vulnerability findings in PRs/IDE Advantages of DevSecOps over DevOps faster delivery improved security posture reduced costs enabling greater overall business access improving security integration and pace enhancing the value of DevOps Container Challenges (Containers are writing OS level things) Increased scope of responsibility Lack of expertise Maintaining velocity Security vulnerabilities can be found in all different areas related to software. Types of Vulnerabilities(Official Lists) CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration Porous Defenses Risky Resource Management Insecure Interaction Between Components OWASP Top 10 A01: Broken Access Control A02: Security Misconfiguration A03: Software Supply Chain Failures A04: Cryptographic Failures A05: Injection A06: Insecure Design A07: Authentication Failures A08: Software or Data Integrity Failures A09: Security Logging and Alerting Failures A10: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions 1.CWE: Common Weakness Enumeration 1.Porous Defenses A porous defenses weakness is one that could allow users to bypass or spoof authentication and authorization processes. Authentication verifies the identity of someone trying to access a system while authorization is set of access and usage permissions assigned to the user. Porous defense weakness examples: Weak password encoding insufficiently protected credentials missing or single factor authentication insecurely inherited permissions sessions that do not expire in a timely manner. Risky Resource Management Risky management of resources such as memory, functions and open-source frameworks. Examples: out of bound read/ write buffer overflow path traversal Insecure Interaction Between Components Many applications today send and receive data across a wide range of services, threads and processes. The way different components interact with each other can introduce vulnerabilities. Examples: cross-site-scripting cross-site request forgery backdoor attacks scripting attacks worms trojan horses other exploits... OWASP Top 10 The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is an open community dedicated to enabling organizations to develop, purchase, and maintain applications and APIs that can be trusted. What are Application Security Risks? Attackers can potentially use many different paths through your application to do harm to your business or organization. Each of these ways poses a potential risk that needs to be investigated. Data Factors to determine application security lists: There are data factors that are listed for each of the Top Ten Categories, here is what they mean: CWEs Mapped: The number of CWEs mapped to a category by the Top Ten team. Incidence Rate: Incidence rate is the percentage of applications vulnerable to that CWE from the population tested by that org for that year. Weighted Exploit: The Exploit sub-score from CVSSv2 and CVSSv3 scores assigned to CVEs mapped to CWEs, normalized, and placed on a 10pt scale. Weighted Impact: The Impact sub-score from CVSSv2 and CVSSv3 scores assigned to CVEs mapped to CWEs, normalized, and placed on a 10pt scale. (Testing) Coverage: The percentage of applications tested by all organizations for a given CWE. Total Occurrences: Total number of applications found to have the CWEs mapped to a category. Total CVEs: Total number of CVEs in the NVD DB that were mapped to the CWEs mapped to a category. Formula: (Max Incidence Rate % \ 1000) + (Max Coverage % \ 100) + (Avg Exploit \ 10) + (Avg Impact \ 20) + (Sum Occurrences / 10000) = Risk Score A01: Broken Access Control Description. Access control enforces policy such that users cannot act outside of their intended permissions. Failures typically lead to unauthorized information disclosure, modification or destruction of all data, or performing a business function outside the user's limits. Common access control vulnerabilities include: Violation of the principle of least privilege, commonly known as deny by default, where access should only be granted for particular capabilities, roles, or users, but is available to anyone. Bypassing access control checks by modifying the URL (parameter tampering or force browsing), internal application state, or the HTML page, or by using an attack tool that modifies API requests. Permitting viewing or editing someone else's account by providing its unique identifier (insecure direct object references) An accessible API with missing access controls for POST, PUT, and DELETE. Elevation of privilege. Acting as a user without being logged in or or gaining privileges beyond those expected of the logged in user (e.g. admin access). Metadata manipulation, such as replaying or tampering with a JSON Web Token (JWT) access control token, a cookie or hidden field manipulated to elevate privileges, or abusing JWT invalidation. CORS misconfiguration allows API access from unauthorized or untrusted origins. Force browsing (guessing URLs) to authenticated pages as an unauthenticated user or to privileged pages as a standard user. How to prevent. Access control is only effective when implemented in trusted server-side code or serverless APIs, where the attacker cannot modify the access control check or metadata. Except for public resources, deny by default. Implement access control mechanisms once and reuse them throughout the application, including minimizing Cross-Origin R

heading: Module 1: Cloud Concepts
text: 1.1 Cloud computing Renting compute, storage, networking and services over the internet, on demand, instead of owning hardware. Shift from CapEx (buy servers upfront) to OpEx (pay as you use). 1.2 Shared responsibility model The provider always owns physical hosts, network and datacenter. You always own your data, identities, and devices/accounts. Everything in between shifts by service type. Layer On-prem IaaS PaaS SaaS - - - - - Data, identities, access You You You You Applications You You You Provider Runtime / middleware You You Provider Provider OS You You Provider Provider Virtual network, hypervisor You Provider Provider Provider Physical hosts, datacenter You Provider Provider Provider 1.3 Cloud models Public: shared Microsoft-owned infrastructure, pay-per-use, no hardware to maintain. Private: dedicated to one organization (on-prem or hosted); more control, higher cost. Hybrid: public + private/on-prem connected (e.g., Azure Arc, ExpressRoute, VPN). Multi-cloud: more than one cloud provider. 1.4 Consumption-based pricing Pay only for what you use (per second/minute/hour, per GB, per million executions). No upfront cost, scale down to stop paying. Example: Azure Functions Consumption plan bills per execution and GB-seconds. 2\. Benefits of the cloud High availability: SLA-backed uptime (e.g., 99.9% = \8.76 hrs downtime/year; 99.99% = \52 min/year). Composite SLA = product of the SLAs of the services in the path. Scalability: Vertical (scale up/down: bigger VM) vs horizontal (scale out/in: more instances). Prefer horizontal for stateless apps. Elasticity: auto-scale in and out with demand. Reliability: resilience via redundancy, self-healing, multi-region design. Predictability: performance (autoscale, load balancing) and cost (calculators, budgets, forecasts). Security and governance: compliance certifications, Azure Policy, Defender for Cloud. Manageability: manage of the cloud (autoscale, templates, monitoring) and in the cloud (Portal, CLI, PowerShell, REST APIs). 3\. Service types You manage Examples Use when - - - - IaaS OS, runtime, apps, data Virtual Machines, VNets, Disks Lift-and-shift, full OS control PaaS Apps and data only App Service, Azure SQL, Functions Build apps without managing servers (most common for devs) SaaS Just use it (config, data) Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365 Ready-made software Serverless (Functions, Logic Apps, Container Apps): PaaS variant where you write code/logic and pay per execution; scale to zero. \---

heading: Module 2: Azure Architecture and Services
text: 4\. Core architecture 4.1 Regions, region pairs, sovereign regions Region: a set of datacenters connected by a low-latency network (e.g., Central India, East US). Pick by latency, compliance/data residency, service availability, and price. Region pair: two regions in the same geography, usually 300+ miles apart. Benefits: sequential platform updates (one at a time), prioritized recovery in a broad outage, and geo-redundant storage replicates to the pair. Sovereign regions: isolated instances for compliance/legal needs: Azure Government (US) and Azure China (21Vianet). 4.2 Availability Zones (AZs) Physically separate datacenters (independent power, cooling, network) within one region; minimum 3 zones in zone-enabled regions. Protect against datacenter-level failure. Zonal services: pin to a specific zone (VMs, disks). Zone-redundant services: replicated across zones automatically (ZRS storage, zone-redundant SQL, Load Balancer Standard). Availability sets (older) protect against rack-level failures within a datacenter via fault/update domains. Prefer zones. 4.3 Datacenters Physical buildings with servers, power, cooling and networking; Microsoft manages them. You never touch them but choose region/zone. 4.4 Resources and resource groups Resource: any manageable item (VM, storage account, VNet). Resource group (RG): logical container for related resources sharing the same lifecycle. A resource lives in exactly one RG; resources can be moved between RGs. RGs can't be nested. Deleting an RG deletes everything in it. RG has a location (for metadata) but its resources can be in other regions. RBAC, policy, tags and locks can be applied at RG level and inherited. 4.5 Hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions Management groups → Subscriptions → Resource groups → Resources Subscription: billing and access boundary; also holds limits/quotas. Common split: dev/test/prod. Management group: container for subscriptions to apply policy/RBAC at scale; up to 6 levels deep (excluding root); one root management group per tenant (Entra tenant). Policy and RBAC assigned at a higher scope are inherited downward. 5\. Compute and networking 5.1 Compute types Type Service Notes - - - Virtual machines Azure VMs, VM Scale Sets IaaS, full control Containers Container Instances (ACI), Container Apps, AKS Lightweight, portable Serverless Functions, Logic Apps Event-driven, pay per execution PaaS web hosting App Service Managed web apps/APIs 5.2 VM options VM sizes/families: General purpose (B, D), Compute-optimized (F), Memory-optimized (E), Storage-optimized (L), GPU (N), HPC (H). Availability Sets: fault domains (power/network) + update domains (planned maintenance). Free; SLA 99.95%. Scale Sets (VMSS): identical VMs, autoscale by metrics/schedule, load-balanced. Azure Virtual Desktop: cloud-hosted Windows desktops/apps. Pricing options: Pay-as-you-go, Reserved Instances (1 or 3 yr, big discount), Savings Plans, Spot VMs (cheap, can be evicted; for interruptible batch work). 5.3 Resources needed for a VM Every VM needs: a resource group, VNet + subnet, NIC (network interface), OS disk (plus optional data disks), and an image/size. Optional: public IP, NSG, load balancer. Stop (deallocate) a VM to stop compute billing, but disks still cost money. 5.4 Application hosting Service Model Best for - - - App Service PaaS Web apps, REST APIs, mobile backends; deployment slots (blue/green), autoscale, built-in TLS; .NET, Java, Node, Python, PHP Azure Functions Serverless Event-driven snippets (HTTP, timer, queue, blob triggers); Consumption, Premium, Dedicated plans Container Instances Serverless containers Quick single containers, no orchestration Container Apps Serverless containers Microservices, KEDA autoscaling, scale to zero AKS Managed Kubernetes Complex orchestration; Azure manages the control plane, you manage nodes/workloads Static Web Apps Static hosting + APIs SPAs (React/Angular) with Functions backend 5.5 Virtual networking VNet: private network in a region; you define address space (CIDR) and subnets. Resources in a VNet talk to each other by default. NSG (Network Security Group): stateful allow/deny rules by IP, port, protocol, priority (lower number = evaluated first); attach to subnet or NIC. Peering: connect VNets (same or different regions) over the Microsoft backbone; not transitive by default. VPN Gateway: encrypted tunnel over the internet (site-to-site, point-to-site). ExpressRoute: private dedicated connection to Azure, not over the public internet; higher reliability and lower latency. Load balancing options: Load Balancer: Layer 4 (TCP/UDP), regional. Application Gateway: Layer 7 (HTTP), regional, with WAF. Front Door: Layer 7, global, CDN + WAF. Traffic Manager: DNS-based global routing. Azure DNS: host DNS zones. Azure Firewall: managed network firewall. Bastion: browser-based RDP/SSH without exposing public IPs. 5.6 Public and private endpoints Public endpoint: service reachable via a public IP/URL (restrict with firewall rules). Private endpoint (Private Link): gives a PaaS service (Storage, SQL, Key Vault) a private IP in your VNet; traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone. Service endpoints extend VNet identity to a service but the service keeps its public endpoint. 6\. Storage 6.1 Storage services (under one Storage Account) Service Use - - Blob Unstructured object data (images, logs, backups, data lake) Files Managed SMB/NFS file shares Queue Simple async messaging (up to 64 KB messages) Table NoSQL key-attribute store Disks VM disks (Managed Disks) 6.2 Access tiers (Blob) Hot (frequent, highest storage cost, lowest access cost) → Cool (30+ days) → Cold (90+ days) → Archive (180+ days, offline, hours to rehydrate). Use lifecycle management policies to move data automatically. 6.3 Redundancy Option Copies Protects from - - - LRS 3 in one datacenter Disk/rack failure ZRS 3 across AZs in one region Datacenter failure GRS LRS + 3 copies in paired region Regional outage GZRS ZRS + copy in paired region Zone + region failure RA-GRS / RA-GZRS As above + read access to secondary Read during outage 6.4 Storage account Globally unique name (3-24 lowercase letters/digits). Types: Standard general-purpose v2 (default), Premium (SSD; block blobs, file shares, page blobs). Secure with Entra ID/RBAC, SAS tokens, firewall/private endpoints, encryption at rest (always on). 6.5 Moving files AzCopy: CLI for fast copy to/from blob and files. Azure Storage Explorer: GUI tool. Azure File Sync: sync on-prem file servers with Azure Files. Azure Data Box: physical device shipped for offline bulk transfer (TBs to PBs). 6.6 Migration Azure Migrate: central hub to discover, assess and migrate servers, databases, web apps. Azure Database Migration Service: migrate databases with minimal downtime. Data Box for offline data (see above). 7\. Identity, access and security 7.1 Directory services Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD): cloud identity provider (users, groups, apps, SSO). Not the same as on-prem AD DS. Entra Domain Services: managed domain services (LDAP, Kerberos, group policy) without running domain controllers. Entra Connect: sync on-prem AD identities to Entra ID (hybrid identity). External ID (B2B/B2C): guest access for partners/customers. 7.2 Authentication methods SSO: sign in once, access many apps. MFA: something you know + have + are. Methods: Authenticator app, FIDO2 keys, SMS/voice (weakest). Passwordless: Windows Hello, Authenticator, FIDO2. SSPR: self-service password reset. Authentication vs authorization: AuthN = who are you; AuthZ = what can you do (OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect are the protocols). 7.3 Conditional Access If-then policies evaluated at sign-in: signals (user, location, device, app, risk) → decision (block, require MFA, require compliant device). Needs Entra ID P1+. 7.4 RBAC Controls what authenticated identities can do on Azure resources. Role assignment = security principal (user/group/service principal/managed identity) + role definition

heading: Module 3: Management and Governance
text: 8\. Cost management 8.1 Factors affecting cost Resource type and size, region, usage/consumption, bandwidth (inbound free; outbound charged), subscription type, reserved vs pay-as-you-go, Azure Hybrid Benefit (bring existing Windows/SQL licenses), Spot pricing, and support plan. 8.2 Pricing Calculator vs TCO Calculator Pricing Calculator: estimate the monthly cost of Azure services you plan to use. TCO Calculator: compare on-prem cost vs Azure over a period (3-5 yrs) to build a migration business case. 8.3 Cost Management + Billing Analyze spend by scope, set budgets, alerts, get forecasts, export data, and see recommendations. 8.4 Tags Key-value metadata on resources/RGs/subscriptions (e.g., env=prod, owner=teamA, costcenter=123) for cost allocation, organization and automation. Not inherited by default; use Azure Policy to enforce/inherit. 9\. Governance and compliance Azure Blueprints: packaged environment definitions (RBAC, policy, ARM templates, RGs). Deprecated by Microsoft; use Template Specs + Deployment Stacks and Azure Policy instead. Still appears in older course material. Azure Policy: creates rules on resources (e.g., allow only certain regions/SKUs, require tags). Effects: Deny, Audit, Append, Modify, DeployIfNotExists. Policy = what resources may look like; RBAC = who may do what. Resource locks: CanNotDelete or ReadOnly on subscription/RG/resource; inherited; override even Owner permissions until removed (only Owner/User Access Admin can remove). Microsoft Purview: data governance/compliance. Service Trust Portal: compliance reports and audits. 10\. Managing and deploying resources Azure Portal: web GUI; good for exploring and one-off tasks. Not repeatable. Cloud Shell: browser-based Bash/PowerShell with CLI preinstalled. Azure CLI (az, cross-platform) and Azure PowerShell (Az module): scriptable, automatable. Azure Arc: extend Azure management (policy, monitoring, Defender) to on-prem, other-cloud servers, Kubernetes and data services. Azure Resource Manager (ARM): the single control plane; every request (Portal, CLI, SDK, REST) goes through it for auth, validation and deployment. Infrastructure as Code: ARM templates (JSON, declarative, idempotent) and Bicep (cleaner DSL that compiles to ARM). Also Terraform. az login az group create -n rg-demo -l centralindia az storage account create -n stdemo12345 -g rg-demo --sku Standard\_LRS az deployment group create -g rg-demo -f main.bicep az group delete -n rg-demo --yes --no-wait 11\. Monitoring Azure Advisor: personalized recommendations in 5 areas: Reliability, Security, Performance, Cost, Operational Excellence. Azure Service Health: personalized view of Azure incidents. Includes Azure Status (global), Service Health (your services/regions), and Resource Health (a specific resource). Azure Monitor: collects metrics and logs across resources. Components: Metrics, Log Analytics (query with KQL), Alerts and action groups, Application Insights (APM for apps: traces, exceptions, dependencies), dashboards/workbooks. \---

heading: Extra Topics Every SDE-1 Should Know
text: Data services Azure SQL Database (managed SQL Server, PaaS); Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL. Cosmos DB: globally distributed NoSQL, multiple APIs, tunable consistency (Strong → Eventual), RU/s throughput. Azure Cache for Redis: in-memory cache for speed. Secrets and identity for apps Never hard-code secrets. Store them in Azure Key Vault (secrets, keys, certificates). Managed Identity: Azure-managed identity for your app, so it authenticates to Key Vault, Storage, SQL with no credentials in code. System-assigned (tied to the resource) or user-assigned (reusable). Service principal: identity for apps/automation (CI/CD) when managed identity isn't possible. Use DefaultAzureCredential in the Azure SDK: works with your login locally and managed identity in Azure. Messaging and integration Service Purpose - - Service Bus Enterprise messaging: queues, topics/subscriptions, ordering, dead-letter Event Grid Reactive events (discrete, "something happened") Event Hubs High-throughput streaming/telemetry ingestion (Kafka-compatible) Storage Queues Simple, cheap queues API Management Publish, secure, throttle APIs Logic Apps Low-code workflows DevOps / CI-CD Azure DevOps (Repos, Pipelines, Boards, Artifacts) or GitHub Actions. Typical flow: commit → build/test → container image to Azure Container Registry (ACR) → deploy to App Service/AKS with staging slots → monitor via Application Insights. Design principles to remember Design for failure: retries with backoff, timeouts, circuit breakers, idempotent operations. Keep services stateless; store state in DB/cache/storage so you can scale out. Use zones for high availability, paired regions/Traffic Manager/Front Door for DR. Tag everything, set budgets, delete unused dev resources (cost hygiene). Least privilege everywhere (RBAC, NSG, managed identities). \---

heading: Git & GitHub
text: A practical guide to everything an entry-level software engineer needs to know about Git and GitHub: concepts, commands, workflows, and the mistakes to avoid. Git vs GitHub Git GitHub --- --- --- What Distributed version control system (VCS) Cloud platform that hosts Git repositories Runs Locally on your machine On the web Does Tracks changes, branches, merges Collaboration: pull requests, issues, code review, CI/CD Alternatives None really (Mercurial, SVN are legacy) GitLab, Bitbucket Why Git? Full history, safe experimentation via branches, offline work, and painless collaboration. --- Installation & Setup # Install sudo apt install git # Debian/Ubuntu brew install git # macOS winget install Git.Git # Windows git --version # Verify One-time configuration git config --global user.name "Your Name" git config --global user.email "you@example.com" git config --global init.defaultBranch main git config --global core.editor "code --wait" # VS Code as editor git config --global pull.rebase false # merge on pull (or true for rebase) git config --list # View all settings git config user.name # View a single value Config levels: --system (all users) → --global (your user) → --local (this repo only; default). SSH authentication with GitHub (recommended) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" # Generate key eval "$(ssh-agent -s)" && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub # Copy → GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys ssh -T git@github.com # Test connection Alternative: HTTPS with a Personal Access Token (PAT). GitHub no longer accepts account passwords for Git operations. --- Core Concepts The three areas Working Directory ──git add──▶ Staging Area (Index) ──git commit──▶ Local Repository ──git push──▶ Remote (GitHub) (your files) (what goes in next commit) (.git history) Key terms Term Meaning --- --- Repository (repo) Project folder tracked by Git (contains a hidden .git/ directory) Commit Snapshot of staged changes with a unique SHA-1 hash, author, timestamp, message Branch A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit HEAD Pointer to your current commit/branch Remote A hosted copy of the repo (conventionally named origin) Upstream The remote branch your local branch tracks Origin Default name for the remote you cloned from Fork Your own server-side copy of someone else's repo Detached HEAD HEAD points to a commit directly, not a branch File states Untracked → Staged → Committed → Modified → Staged → ... --- Starting a Repository git init # Create a new repo in current folder git init my-project # Create in a new folder git clone <url> # Copy a remote repo locally git clone <url> my-folder # Clone into a named folder git clone --depth 1 <url> # Shallow clone (latest commit only; fast) git clone -b <branch> <url> # Clone a specific branch --- Daily Workflow: Stage, Commit, Inspect Check status and differences git status # Current state of working dir and staging area git status -s # Short format git diff # Unstaged changes git diff --staged # Staged changes (what will be committed) git diff main..feature # Compare two branches git diff <commit1> <commit2> # Compare two commits Stage changes git add file.txt # Stage a file git add src/ # Stage a directory git add . # Stage everything in current directory git add -p # Interactively stage chunks (hunks); great for clean commits git rm file.txt # Delete file and stage the deletion git rm --cached file.txt # Untrack file but keep it on disk git mv old.txt new.txt # Rename/move and stage Commit git commit -m "Add login validation" # Commit with message git commit -am "Fix typo" # Stage tracked files + commit (skips new files) git commit --amend -m "Better message" # Rewrite the last commit message git commit --amend --no-edit # Add staged changes to the last commit View history git log # Full history git log --oneline # One line per commit git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate # Visual branch graph git log -n 5 # Last 5 commits git log --author="Name" # Filter by author git log --since="2 weeks ago" # Filter by date git log -p file.txt # History with diffs for one file git log --grep="bug" # Search commit messages git show <commit> # Details and diff of one commit git blame file.txt # Who last changed each line --- Branching Branches let you work on features or fixes in isolation without touching main. git branch # List local branches (* = current) git branch -a # List local and remote branches git branch -vv # Show tracking info and last commit git branch feature/login # Create branch git switch feature/login # Switch to branch (modern) git switch -c feature/login # Create and switch git checkout feature/login # Switch (older equivalent) git checkout -b feature/login # Create and switch (older equivalent) git branch -m new-name # Rename current branch git branch -d feature/login # Delete (only if merged) git branch -D feature/login # Force delete git push origin --delete feature/login # Delete remote branch --- Merging & Rebasing Both integrate changes from one branch into another, differently. Merge git switch main git merge feature/login # Merge feature into main git merge --no-ff feature/login # Always create a merge commit git merge --squash feature/login # Combine all commits into one staged change git merge --abort # Cancel an in-progress merge Fast-forward: main hasn't moved, so Git just advances the pointer (no merge commit). Three-way merge: both branches diverged, so Git creates a merge commit. Rebase Replays your commits on top of another branch for a linear history. git switch feature/login git rebase main # Replay feature commits on top of latest main git rebase --continue # After resolving conflicts git rebase --abort # Cancel rebase git rebase -i HEAD~3 # Interactive: squash, reword, reorder, drop last 3 commits Interactive rebase keywords: pick, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop. Merge vs Rebase Merge Rebase --- --- --- History Preserves true history (non-linear) Linear, cleaner Safety Non-destructive Rewrites commits (new hashes) Use for Integrating into shared branches Cleaning up your own local/feature branch Golden rule: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch. --- Resolving Merge Conflicts Conflicts occur when two branches edit the same lines. <<<<<<< HEAD your current branch's version ======= incoming branch's version >>>>>>> feature/login Steps: git status # See conflicted files ("both modified") # 1. Open the files, choose/combine the correct code, delete the markers git add <resolved-file> # 2. Mark as resolved git commit # 3. Complete the merge (or: git rebase --continue) git checkout --ours file.txt # Take your version git checkout --theirs file.txt # Take the incoming version git mergetool # Launch a configured merge tool --- Working with Remotes git remote -v # List remotes git remote add origin <url> # Add a remote git remote set-url origin <new-url> # Change remote URL git remote remove origin # Remove a remote git fetch # Download changes, don't merge git fetch --prune # Also remove stale remote-tracking branches git pull # fetch + merge (or rebase) into current branch git pull --rebase # fetch + rebase git push origin main # Push branch git push -u origin feature/login # Push and set upstream (first push) git push # Push to the tracked upstream git push --force-with-lease # Safer force push (fails if remote changed) Fork workflow (open source) git remote add upstream <original-repo-url> # Link the original repo git fetch upstream git switch main git merge upstream/main # Sync your fork with the original git push origin main Prefer --force-with-lease over --force. Never force-push to main. --- Undoing Things Choose the right tool depending on what you want to undo. Situation Command --- --- Discard unstaged changes in a file git restore file.txt Unstage a file (keep changes) git restore --staged file.txt Fix the last commit message git commit --amend Undo last commit, keep changes staged git reset --soft HEAD1 Undo last commit, keep changes

async executes the script the moment it finishes downloading (which pauses HTML parsing), whereas defer waits for the HTML parsing to completely finish before executing the script in the order it appears on the page. DEFAULT script tag: HTML parsing is paused for download and execution The scripts are executed immediately upon discovery/ arrival Execution Order: The scripts are executed in an ordered manner(as they appear in HTML). DOM Dependent? : Safe(if placed at the bottom) script async tag: HTML parsing is paused only during execution. The scripts are executed immediately after download completes. Execution Order: Unordered(load-first basis) DOM Dependent? : Unsafe(may run before DOM is ready) script defer tag: HTML Parsing is never paused. The scripts are executed after the DOM is fully parsed. Execution Order: Ordered(as they appear in HTML) DOM Dependent? : Safe(always runs after dom is ready) When to Use Which Use async when: The script is completely independent. It does not rely on other scripts. It does not need to manipulate the DOM. Examples: Analytics tools like Google Analytics, ad tracking pixels, or heatmaps. Use defer when: The script relies on the full DOM being built. The script depends on, or is depended on by, another script. Examples: UI interaction scripts, application bootloaders, or frameworks like React or Vue packages.

text: An array is an ordered collection of values stored under numeric indexes, starting at 0. Arrays can hold values of any type, including other arrays and objects.

heading: Creating Arrays
text: const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "mango"]; const empty = []; const mixed = [1, "two", true, null, { a: 1 }]; const fromConstructor = new Array(3); // [ <3 empty items> ] const filled = Array.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i); // [0, 1, 2]

heading: Accessing and Updating
text: fruits[0]; // "apple" fruits[fruits.length - 1]; // "mango" fruits.at(-1); // "mango" fruits[1] = "grape"; // update fruits.length; // 3

heading: Adding and Removing Elements
text: Method Action --- --- push(x) Add to the end pop() Remove from the end unshift(x) Add to the start shift() Remove from the start splice(i, n, ...items) Remove/insert at an index const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.push(4); // [1, 2, 3, 4] nums.pop(); // [1, 2, 3] nums.unshift(0); // [0, 1, 2, 3] nums.shift(); // [1, 2, 3] nums.splice(1, 1); // removes 2 -> [1, 3] nums.splice(1, 0, 2); // inserts 2 -> [1, 2, 3]

heading: Searching
text: const nums = [10, 20, 30, 20]; nums.indexOf(20); // 1 nums.lastIndexOf(20); // 3 nums.includes(30); // true nums.find(n => n > 15); // 20 nums.findIndex(n => n > 15); // 1

heading: Iterating
text: const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.forEach(n => console.log(n)); for (const n of nums) console.log(n);

heading: Transforming
text: const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; nums.map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4] nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 15 nums.some(n => n > 4); // true nums.every(n => n > 0); // true

heading: Slicing, Joining, and Sorting
text: const nums = [3, 1, 2]; nums.slice(0, 2); // [3, 1] (does not modify original) nums.concat([4, 5]); // [3, 1, 2, 4, 5] [...nums, 4, 5]; // spread alternative nums.join("-"); // "3-1-2" nums.reverse(); // [2, 1, 3] (modifies original) nums.sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 3] (modifies original) sort() without a compare function sorts values as strings.

heading: Destructuring and Spread
text: const [first, second, ...rest] = [1, 2, 3, 4]; // first = 1, second = 2, rest = [3, 4] const copy = [...rest];

heading: Checking for an Array
text: Array.isArray([1, 2]); // true Array.isArray("abc"); // false

heading: Callback Function in JavaScript
text: A callback function is a function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later by that function.

heading: Basic Example
text: function greet(name, callback) { console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); callback(); } function done() { console.log("Greeting finished."); } greet("Sam", done); // Hello, Sam! // Greeting finished.

heading: Inline and Arrow Callbacks
text: greet("Sam", function () { console.log("Done"); }); greet("Sam", () => console.log("Done"));

heading: Callbacks with Arguments
text: function calculate(a, b, operation) { return operation(a, b); } calculate(2, 3, (x, y) => x + y); // 5 calculate(2, 3, (x, y) => x * y); // 6

heading: Callbacks in Built-in Methods
text: Many array methods accept callbacks. const nums = [1, 2, 3]; nums.map(n => n * 2); nums.filter(n => n > 1); nums.forEach(n => console.log(n));

heading: Synchronous Callbacks
text: Called immediately, in order, while the main function is running. [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n));

heading: Asynchronous Callbacks
text: Called later, after an operation finishes. console.log("Start"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Callback after 1 second"); }, 1000); console.log("End"); // Start // End // Callback after 1 second

heading: Error-First Callbacks
text: A common convention where the first argument of the callback is an error (or null). function fetchData(callback) { const success = true; if (success) { callback(null, { id: 1 }); } else { callback(new Error("Failed to fetch")); } } fetchData((error, data) => { if (error) { console.error(error.message); return; } console.log(data); });

heading: Callback Hell
text: Nesting many callbacks makes code hard to read and maintain. step1(function (result1) { step2(result1, function (result2) { step3(result2, function (result3) { console.log(result3); }); }); }); Ways to avoid it: use named functions, keep nesting shallow, or use Promises and async/await.

heading: Key Points
text: A callback is just a regular function passed as a value. Pass the function itself, not its result: greet("Sam", done), not greet("Sam", done()). Callbacks can run synchronously or asynchronously.

heading: Closures in JavaScript
text: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the scope where it was created, even after that outer scope has finished executing.

heading: Basic Example
text: function outer() { const message = "Hello"; function inner() { console.log(message); } return inner; } const fn = outer(); fn(); // "Hello" inner still has access to message even though outer has already returned.

heading: Counter Example
text: function createCounter() { let count = 0; return function () { count++; return count; }; } const counter = createCounter(); counter(); // 1 counter(); // 2 counter(); // 3 Each call to createCounter() creates its own separate count. const a = createCounter(); const b = createCounter(); a(); // 1 a(); // 2 b(); // 1

heading: Data Privacy
text: Closures can hide variables so they cannot be accessed directly from outside. function createAccount(balance) { return { deposit(amount) { balance += amount; return balance; }, getBalance() { return balance; }, }; } const account = createAccount(100); account.deposit(50); // 150 account.getBalance(); // 150 account.balance; // undefined

heading: Function Factories
text: function multiplier(factor) { return (number) => number * factor; } const double = multiplier(2); const triple = multiplier(3); double(5); // 10 triple(5); // 15

heading: Closures in Loops
text: With var, all callbacks share the same variable. for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } // 3, 3, 3 With let, each iteration gets its own variable. for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 100); } // 0, 1, 2

heading: Lexical Scope
text: A closure works because of lexical scoping: a function can access variables from the scope where it was written, not where it is called. const x = "global"; function show() { console.log(x); } function run() { const x = "local"; show(); } run(); // "global"

heading: Key Points
text: Every function in JavaScript forms a closure over its surrounding scope. Closures keep variables alive as long as the function exists. Common uses: private variables, function factories, callbacks, and event handlers.

heading: Functions in JavaScript
text: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a task. It can accept inputs (parameters) and return an output.

heading: Function Declaration
text: function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } greet("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!" Function declarations are hoisted, so they can be called before they are defined.

heading: Function Expression
text: const greet = function (name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; }; Function expressions are not hoisted.

heading: Arrow Function
text: const greet = (name) => `Hello, ${name}!`; const add = (a, b) => a + b; const square = n => n * n; const log = () => { console.log("No parameters"); }; Arrow functions do not have their own this.

heading: Parameters and Arguments
text: function add(a, b) { // a, b are parameters return a + b; } add(2, 3); // 2, 3 are arguments

heading: Default Parameters
text: function greet(name = "Guest") { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } greet(); // "Hello, Guest!" greet("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!"

heading: Rest Parameters
text: Collects any number of arguments into an array. function sum(...numbers) { return numbers.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0); } sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10

heading: Return Value
text: A function returns undefined if there is no return statement. A return ends the function immediately. function check(n) { if (n > 0) return "positive"; return "not positive"; }

heading: Returning Multiple Values
text: function minMax(arr) { return [Math.min(...arr), Math.max(...arr)]; } const [min, max] = minMax([3, 1, 2]);

heading: Immediately Invoked Function Expression (IIFE)
text: A function that runs as soon as it is defined. (function () { console.log("Runs immediately"); })();

heading: Scope
text: Variables declared inside a function are not accessible outside it. function demo() { const inside = "local"; } // inside is not accessible here

heading: Recursion
text: A function that calls itself. function factorial(n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); } factorial(5); // 120

heading: Methods
text: A function stored as an object property. const user = { name: "Sam", sayHi() { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; }, }; user.sayHi();

heading: Functions as Values
text: Functions are first-class: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments, and returned from other functions. const operations = { add: (a, b) => a + b, multiply: (a, b) => a * b, }; operations.add(2, 3); // 5

heading: Loops in JavaScript
text: Loops run a block of code repeatedly until a condition is no longer met.

heading: for
text: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 } Syntax: for (initialization; condition; update) { ... }

heading: while
text: Runs while the condition is true. The condition is checked before each iteration. let i = 0; while (i < 5) { console.log(i); i++; }

heading: do...while
text: Runs the block at least once, then checks the condition. let i = 0; do { console.log(i); i++; } while (i < 5);

heading: for...of
text: Iterates over the values of iterable objects such as arrays and strings. for (const fruit of ["apple", "banana"]) { console.log(fruit); } for (const char of "hi") { console.log(char); }

heading: for...in
text: Iterates over the enumerable property keys of an object. const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25 }; for (const key in user) { console.log(key, user[key]); } Prefer for...of for arrays. for...in is meant for objects.

heading: forEach
text: An array method that runs a function for each element. [1, 2, 3].forEach((n, index) => { console.log(index, n); });

heading: break
text: Exits the loop immediately. for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) { if (i === 3) break; console.log(i); // 0, 1, 2 }

heading: continue
text: Skips the rest of the current iteration. for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) { if (i === 2) continue; console.log(i); // 0, 1, 3, 4 }

heading: Nested Loops
text: for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { for (let j = 1; j <= 3; j++) { console.log(`${i} x ${j} = ${i * j}`); } }

heading: Labels
text: A label lets break or continue target an outer loop. outer: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) { if (j === 1) continue outer; console.log(i, j); } }

heading: Infinite Loops
text: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever. Always make sure the condition changes. while (true) { // must contain a break to stop break; }

heading: setInterval in JavaScript
text: setInterval() repeatedly runs a function at a fixed time interval (in milliseconds) until it is stopped.

heading: Syntax
text: setInterval(callback, interval, arg1, arg2, ...); Parameter Description --- --- callback The function to run repeatedly interval Time between each call in milliseconds arg1, arg2, ... Optional arguments passed to the callback It returns an ID (in browsers, a number) that identifies the interval.

heading: Basic Example
text: setInterval(() => { console.log("Runs every 1 second"); }, 1000);

heading: Stopping with clearInterval
text: const intervalId = setInterval(() => { console.log("Tick"); }, 1000); clearInterval(intervalId);

heading: Stopping After a Number of Runs
text: let count = 0; const intervalId = setInterval(() => { count++; console.log(`Run ${count}`); if (count === 5) { clearInterval(intervalId); } }, 1000);

heading: Passing Arguments
text: function greet(name) { console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`); } setInterval(greet, 2000, "Sam");

heading: Countdown Example
text: let seconds = 5; const timer = setInterval(() => { console.log(seconds); seconds--; if (seconds < 0) { clearInterval(timer); console.log("Done!"); } }, 1000);

heading: Clock Example
text: setInterval(() => { console.log(new Date().toLocaleTimeString()); }, 1000);

heading: Stopping After a Delay
text: const id = setInterval(() => console.log("Tick"), 1000); setTimeout(() => clearInterval(id), 5000); // stops after 5 seconds

heading: Key Points
text: The first call happens after the first interval, not immediately. The interval keeps running until clearInterval(id) is called. The interval is a minimum time; busy code can delay each run. Always store the ID so the interval can be cleared.

heading: setTimeout in JavaScript
text: setTimeout() runs a function once after a specified delay (in milliseconds).

heading: Syntax
text: setTimeout(callback, delay, arg1, arg2, ...); Parameter Description --- --- callback The function to run after the delay delay Time to wait in milliseconds (default 0) arg1, arg2, ... Optional arguments passed to the callback It returns a numeric ID (in browsers) that identifies the timer.

heading: Basic Example
text: setTimeout(() => { console.log("Runs after 2 seconds"); }, 2000);

heading: Passing Arguments
text: function greet(name, message) { console.log(`${message}, ${name}!`); } setTimeout(greet, 1000, "Sam", "Hello"); // Hello, Sam!

heading: Using a Named Function
text: function sayHi() { console.log("Hi!"); } setTimeout(sayHi, 1000); // pass the function, do not call it

heading: Cancelling with clearTimeout
text: const timerId = setTimeout(() => { console.log("This will not run"); }, 3000); clearTimeout(timerId);

heading: Asynchronous Behavior
text: setTimeout does not block the code that follows it. console.log("Start"); setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 1000); console.log("End"); // Start // End // Timeout

heading: Zero Delay
text: Even with a delay of 0, the callback runs after the current code finishes. setTimeout(() => console.log("Timeout"), 0); console.log("Sync"); // Sync // Timeout

heading: The this Keyword
text: In a regular function callback, this is not the surrounding object. Use an arrow function to keep it. const user = { name: "Sam", greet() { setTimeout(() => { console.log(`Hi, ${this.name}`); }, 1000); }, }; user.greet(); // Hi, Sam

heading: Chaining Delays
text: setTimeout(() => { console.log("Step 1"); setTimeout(() => { console.log("Step 2"); }, 1000); }, 1000);

heading: Key Points
text: The delay is a minimum wait time, not a guaranteed exact time. It runs the callback only once. Use clearTimeout(id) to cancel a pending timer.

heading: Strings in JavaScript
text: A string is a sequence of characters used to represent text. Strings are immutable: methods return a new string instead of changing the original.

heading: Creating Strings
text: const single = 'Hello'; const double = "Hello"; const template = `Hello`; const fromConstructor = String(123); // "123"

heading: Template Literals
text: const name = "Sam"; const age = 25; `My name is ${name} and I am ${age}.`; `Line one Line two`; // multi-line

heading: Length and Character Access
text: const str = "JavaScript"; str.length; // 10 str[0]; // "J" str.charAt(4); // "S" str.at(-1); // "t"

heading: Changing Case
text: "hello".toUpperCase(); // "HELLO" "HELLO".toLowerCase(); // "hello"

heading: Searching
text: const str = "Hello, World"; str.indexOf("o"); // 4 str.lastIndexOf("o"); // 8 str.includes("World"); // true str.startsWith("Hello"); // true str.endsWith("World"); // true str.search(/W/); // 7

heading: Extracting Parts
text: const str = "JavaScript"; str.slice(0, 4); // "Java" str.slice(-6); // "Script" str.substring(4, 10); // "Script"

heading: Replacing
text: "a-b-c".replace("-", "+"); // "a+b-c" "a-b-c".replaceAll("-", "+"); // "a+b+c" "a1b2".replace(/\d/g, "#"); // "a#b#"

heading: Trimming and Padding
text: " hi ".trim(); // "hi" " hi ".trimStart(); // "hi " " hi ".trimEnd(); // " hi" "5".padStart(3, "0"); // "005" "5".padEnd(3, "0"); // "500"

heading: Repeating and Concatenating
text: "ab".repeat(3); // "ababab" "Hello" + " " + "World"; // "Hello World" "Hello".concat(" World"); // "Hello World"

heading: Comparing
text: "a" === "a"; // true "apple" < "banana"; // true "a".localeCompare("b"); // -1

heading: Escape Characters
text: Sequence Meaning --- --- \n New line \t Tab \\ Backslash \' Single quote \" Double quote

heading: Iterating Over a String
text: for (const char of "abc") { console.log(char); }

heading: call, apply, bind in JavaScript
text: call, apply, and bind are function methods used to set the value of this explicitly when invoking a function.

heading: The Problem
text: const user = { name: "Sam", greet(greeting) { return `${greeting}, ${this.name}`; }, }; const greet = user.greet; greet("Hello"); // `this` is lost -> "Hello, undefined"

heading: call()
text: Calls the function immediately with a given this and arguments passed individually. function greet(greeting, punctuation) { return `${greeting}, ${this.name}${punctuation}`; } const person = { name: "Sam" }; greet.call(person, "Hello", "!"); // "Hello, Sam!" Syntax: func.call(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...)

heading: apply()
text: Same as call(), but arguments are passed as an array. greet.apply(person, ["Hello", "!"]); // "Hello, Sam!" Syntax: func.apply(thisArg, [argsArray]) Math.max.apply(null, [3, 7, 2]); // 7

heading: bind()
text: Returns a new function with this permanently set. It does not call the function immediately. const greetSam = greet.bind(person); greetSam("Hello", "!"); // "Hello, Sam!" Syntax: const newFunc = func.bind(thisArg, arg1, arg2, ...)

heading: Partial Application with bind
text: function multiply(a, b) { return a * b; } const double = multiply.bind(null, 2); double(5); // 10

heading: Borrowing Methods
text: const user1 = { name: "Sam", sayHi() { return `Hi, ${this.name}`; }, }; const user2 = { name: "Alex" }; user1.sayHi.call(user2); // "Hi, Alex"

heading: Fixing this in Callbacks
text: const counter = { count: 0, start() { setTimeout( function () { this.count++; console.log(this.count); }.bind(this), 1000 ); }, }; counter.start(); // 1

heading: Comparison
text: Method Calls immediately Arguments Returns --- --- --- --- call Yes Individually Function result apply Yes As an array Function result bind No Individually (optional) New function

heading: Async & Await in JavaScript
text: async and await provide a cleaner way to work with Promises, letting asynchronous code be written in a synchronous style.

heading: async Function
text: An async function always returns a Promise. async function greet() { return "Hello"; } greet().then(console.log); // "Hello" Returning a value wraps it in a resolved Promise. Throwing an error returns a rejected Promise.

heading: await
text: await pauses the execution of an async function until the Promise settles, then returns its resolved value. function delay(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); } async function run() { console.log("Start"); await delay(1000); console.log("After 1 second"); } run(); await can only be used inside an async function (or at the top level of an ES module).

heading: Fetching Data
text: async function getUser() { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/user"); const data = await response.json(); return data; }

heading: Error Handling with try...catch
text: async function getUser() { try { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/user"); if (!response.ok) { throw new Error("Request failed"); } return await response.json(); } catch (error) { console.error(error.message); } finally { console.log("Done"); } }

heading: Sequential Execution
text: Each await waits for the previous one to finish. async function sequential() { const a = await taskA(); // waits const b = await taskB(); // then runs return [a, b]; }

heading: Parallel Execution
text: Start the tasks first, then await them together. async function parallel() { const [a, b] = await Promise.all([taskA(), taskB()]); return [a, b]; }

heading: async Arrow Functions
text: const fetchData = async () => { const response = await fetch("https://api.example.com/data"); return response.json(); };

heading: await in Loops
text: async function processItems(items) { for (const item of items) { await process(item); // one at a time } }

heading: Key Points
text: async makes a function return a Promise. await waits for a Promise without blocking the rest of the program. Use try...catch to handle rejected Promises. Use Promise.all to run independent tasks in parallel.

heading: Promise in JavaScript
text: A Promise is an object that represents the eventual completion (or failure) of an asynchronous operation and its resulting value.

heading: States
text: State Meaning --- --- pending Initial state, not yet finished fulfilled Operation completed successfully rejected Operation failed Once a Promise is fulfilled or rejected, it is settled and its state cannot change.

heading: Creating a Promise
text: const promise = new Promise((resolve, reject) => { const success = true; if (success) { resolve("Operation succeeded"); } else { reject(new Error("Operation failed")); } }); resolve(value) marks the Promise as fulfilled. reject(error) marks the Promise as rejected.

heading: Consuming a Promise
text: promise .then(result => console.log(result)) .catch(error => console.error(error.message)) .finally(() => console.log("Finished")); Method Runs when --- --- then() The Promise is fulfilled catch() The Promise is rejected finally() The Promise settles, either way

heading: Asynchronous Example
text: function delay(ms) { return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms)); } delay(1000).then(() => console.log("1 second passed"));

heading: Promise Chaining
text: Each then() returns a new Promise, so calls can be chained. Promise.resolve(1) .then(n => n + 1) // 2 .then(n => n * 2) // 4 .then(n => console.log(n)); // 4 A value returned from then() is passed to the next then(). A returned Promise is awaited before continuing.

heading: Error Handling in Chains
text: An error thrown anywhere in the chain skips to the nearest catch(). Promise.resolve() .then(() => { throw new Error("Something went wrong"); }) .then(() => console.log("Skipped")) .catch(error => console.error(error.message));

heading: Shortcuts
text: Promise.resolve("done"); // already fulfilled Promise.reject(new Error("failed")); // already rejected

heading: Callbacks vs Promises
text: // Callbacks getData(function (a) { getMore(a, function (b) { console.log(b); }); }); // Promises getData() .then(a => getMore(a)) .then(b => console.log(b));

heading: Key Points
text: A Promise is either pending, fulfilled, or rejected. Use then, catch, and finally to handle the result. Chaining avoids deeply nested callbacks. Always handle rejections with catch().

heading: Promise APIs in JavaScript
text: The Promise object provides static methods for working with multiple Promises at once.

heading: Promise.all()
text: Waits for all Promises to fulfill. Rejects immediately if any Promise rejects. const p1 = Promise.resolve(1); const p2 = Promise.resolve(2); const p3 = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(3), 1000)); Promise.all([p1, p2, p3]).then(results => { console.log(results); // [1, 2, 3] }); Promise.all([p1, Promise.reject(new Error("Failed")), p3]) .catch(error => console.error(error.message)); // "Failed" Returns an array of results in the same order as the input. Fails fast on the first rejection.

heading: Promise.allSettled()
text: Waits for all Promises to settle, whether fulfilled or rejected. It never rejects. Promise.allSettled([ Promise.resolve("ok"), Promise.reject(new Error("failed")), ]).then(results => console.log(results)); // [ // { status: "fulfilled", value: "ok" }, // { status: "rejected", reason: Error: failed } // ]

heading: Promise.race()
text: Settles as soon as the first Promise settles (fulfilled or rejected). const slow = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("slow"), 2000)); const fast = new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("fast"), 500)); Promise.race([slow, fast]).then(result => console.log(result)); // "fast" Common use: adding a timeout to an operation. const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("Timed out")), 3000) ); Promise.race([fetch("https://api.example.com/data"), timeout]);

heading: Promise.any()
text: Fulfills as soon as the first Promise fulfills. Ignores rejections unless all Promises reject. Promise.any([ Promise.reject(new Error("fail 1")), Promise.resolve("success"), Promise.reject(new Error("fail 2")), ]).then(result => console.log(result)); // "success" If all Promises reject, it rejects with an AggregateError. Promise.any([ Promise.reject(new Error("fail 1")), Promise.reject(new Error("fail 2")), ]).catch(error => { console.log(error.name); // "AggregateError" console.log(error.errors.length); // 2 });

heading: Promise.resolve()
text: Returns a Promise that is fulfilled with the given value. Promise.resolve("done").then(console.log); // "done"

heading: Promise.reject()
text: Returns a Promise that is rejected with the given reason. Promise.reject(new Error("failed")).catch(error => console.error(error.message));

heading: Comparison
text: Method Fulfills when Rejects when --- --- --- Promise.all All fulfill Any one rejects Promise.allSettled All settle Never Promise.race First settles with fulfillment First settles with rejection Promise.any Any one fulfills All reject

heading: Debouncing in JavaScript
text: Debouncing is a technique that delays running a function until a specified time has passed since the last time it was called. If the function is called again before the delay ends, the timer resets.

heading: Explanation
text: Imagine a user typing in a search box. Without debouncing, an API request would fire on every keystroke. With debouncing, the request fires only after the user stops typing for a set time (for example, 500ms). Keystrokes: a b c d e (pause) Timer: reset reset reset reset reset --> runs once

heading: Common Use Cases
text: Search box suggestions Auto-saving a form Window resize handlers Validating input after the user stops typing

heading: Basic Implementation
text: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timerId; return function (...args) { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => { fn.apply(this, args); }, delay); }; } How it works: timerId is kept in a closure, so it persists between calls. Each call clears the previous timer. A new timer starts, and the function runs only if no new call arrives within delay.

heading: Usage
text: function search(query) { console.log("Searching for:", query); } const debouncedSearch = debounce(search, 500); debouncedSearch("j"); debouncedSearch("ja"); debouncedSearch("jav"); // Only "Searching for: jav" is logged, 500ms after the last call

heading: With an Input Event
text: const input = document.querySelector("#search"); input.addEventListener( "input", debounce((event) => { console.log(event.target.value); }, 500) );

heading: Leading Edge Option
text: Run the function immediately on the first call, then ignore calls until the delay passes without activity. function debounce(fn, delay, immediate = false) { let timerId; return function (...args) { const callNow = immediate && !timerId; clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => { timerId = null; if (!immediate) fn.apply(this, args); }, delay); if (callNow) fn.apply(this, args); }; } const onClick = debounce(() => console.log("Clicked"), 1000, true);

heading: Adding a Cancel Method
text: function debounce(fn, delay) { let timerId; function debounced(...args) { clearTimeout(timerId); timerId = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), delay); } debounced.cancel = () => clearTimeout(timerId); return debounced; } const save = debounce(() => console.log("Saved"), 1000); save(); save.cancel(); // nothing is logged

heading: Key Points
text: Debouncing runs the function only after calls stop for the given delay. Each new call resets the timer. It is implemented with setTimeout, clearTimeout, and a closure.

heading: Event Bubbling & Trickling (Capturing) in JavaScript
text: When an event happens on an element, it travels through the DOM tree in phases. Understanding these phases explains why a click on a child can trigger handlers on its parents.

id: JavaScript/DOM & DOM Manipulation/Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling/Event-Bubbling-Trickling
topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Propagation Phases
text: Capturing (trickling) phase: the event travels down from window to the target element. Target phase: the event reaches the target element. Bubbling phase: the event travels back up from the target to window.

id: JavaScript/DOM & DOM Manipulation/Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling/Event-Bubbling-Trickling
topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Bubbling (Default)
text: By default, event listeners run in the bubbling phase. The innermost element's handler runs first, then its parents'. document.getElementById("grandparent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("grandparent"); }); document.getElementById("parent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("parent"); }); document.getElementById("child").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("child"); }); // Clicking the button logs: // child // parent // grandparent

id: JavaScript/DOM & DOM Manipulation/Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling/Event-Bubbling-Trickling
topic: DOM & DOM Manipulation › Event Bubbling, Capturing aka Trickling
heading: Event Trickling (Capturing)
text: Pass true (or { capture: true }) as the third argument to listen during the capturing phase. Outer elements run first. document.getElementById("grandparent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("grandparent"); }, true); document.getElementById("parent").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("parent"); }, true); document.getElementById("child").addEventListener("click", () => { console.log("child"); }, true); // Clicking the button logs: // grandparent // parent // child

heading: Capturing and Bubbling Together
text: Capturing listeners always run before bubbling listeners for the same event. parent.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("parent capture"), true); parent.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("parent bubble"), false); child.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("child")); // Clicking the child logs: // parent capture // child // parent bubble

heading: Key Points
text: Order of propagation: capturing (down) → target → bubbling (up). Listeners use bubbling by default; pass true to use capturing. event.target is the origin of the event; event.currentTarget is where the listener is attached. stopPropagation() stops the event from traveling further.

heading: Event Delegation in JavaScript
text: Event delegation is a technique where a single event listener is attached to a parent element to handle events for all of its children, including children added later. It works because of event bubbling.

heading: The Problem: One Listener per Element
text: const items = document.querySelectorAll("#list li"); items.forEach((item) => { item.addEventListener("click", () => { console.log(item.textContent); }); }); This creates many listeners and does not work for items added later.

heading: The Solution: Delegation
text:
• Item 1
  • Item 2
  • Item 3
const list = document.querySelector("#list"); list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { if (event.target.tagName === "LI") { console.log(event.target.textContent); } }); One listener handles clicks for every li, including ones added dynamically. const newItem = document.createElement("li"); newItem.textContent = "Item 4"; list.appendChild(newItem); // clicking it works automatically

heading: Using closest()
text:
If the clickable element contains child elements, event.target may be an inner element. Use closest() to find the intended element.
  • Item 1
  • Item 2
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { const button = event.target.closest("button"); if (!button || !list.contains(button)) return; const li = button.closest("li"); console.log("Deleting item", li.dataset.id); li.remove(); });

heading: Using matches()
text: list.addEventListener("click", (event) => { if (event.target.matches("li.active")) { console.log("Active item clicked"); } });

heading: Handling Multiple Actions
text: const actions = { save() { console.log("Saving"); }, edit() { console.log("Editing"); }, delete() { console.log("Deleting"); }, }; document.querySelector("#toolbar").addEventListener("click", (event) => { const action = event.target.dataset.action; if (action && actions[action]) { actions[action](); } });

heading: Benefits
text: Fewer event listeners, so less memory use. Works for elements added or removed dynamically. Less code to set up and clean up.

heading: Limitations
text: Only works for events that bubble (not focus, blur, etc.; use focusin and focusout instead). If a child calls event.stopPropagation(), the parent listener will not run. Very generic listeners high in the tree, such as on document, can add unnecessary work.

heading: Key Points
text: Attach the listener to a common parent. Use event.target to find which child triggered the event. Use closest() when the target may be a nested element.

heading: Function Currying in JavaScript
text: Currying is a technique that transforms a function taking multiple arguments into a sequence of functions that each take a single argument. f(a, b, c) becomes f(a)(b)(c)

heading: Basic Example
text: // Normal function function add(a, b) { return a + b; } add(2, 3); // 5 // Curried function function curriedAdd(a) { return function (b) { return a + b; }; } curriedAdd(2)(3); // 5

heading: Arrow Function Version
text: const add = a => b => a + b; add(2)(3); // 5

heading: Three Arguments
text: const volume = l => w => h => l * w * h; volume(2)(3)(4); // 24

heading: Partial Application
text: A curried function can be called with some arguments now and the rest later. const multiply = a => b => a * b; const double = multiply(2); const triple = multiply(3); double(5); // 10 triple(5); // 15

heading: Why Currying Works: Closures
text: Each inner function remembers the arguments from the outer functions through closure. function greet(greeting) { return function (name) { return `${greeting}, ${name}!`; }; } const sayHello = greet("Hello"); sayHello("Sam"); // "Hello, Sam!" sayHello("Alex"); // "Hello, Alex!"

heading: Generic curry Function
text: function curry(fn) { return function curried(...args) { if (args.length >= fn.length) { return fn.apply(this, args); } return function (...nextArgs) { return curried.apply(this, [...args, ...nextArgs]); }; }; } function sum(a, b, c) { return a + b + c; } const curriedSum = curry(sum); curriedSum(1)(2)(3); // 6 curriedSum(1, 2)(3); // 6 curriedSum(1)(2, 3); // 6 curriedSum(1, 2, 3); // 6 fn.length is the number of parameters the original function expects.

heading: Practical Example
text: const log = level => message => `[${level}] ${message}`; const info = log("INFO"); const error = log("ERROR"); info("Server started"); // "[INFO] Server started" error("Server crashed"); // "[ERROR] Server crashed"

heading: With Array Methods
text: const isGreaterThan = limit => n => n > limit; [1, 5, 10, 15].filter(isGreaterThan(8)); // [10, 15]

heading: Currying vs Partial Application
text: Currying Partial Application --- --- Converts f(a, b, c) into f(a)(b)(c) Fixes some arguments and returns a function for the rest Each function takes one argument Returned function can take any number of arguments

heading: Key Points
text: Currying turns a multi-argument function into nested single-argument functions. It relies on closures to remember earlier arguments. It helps create reusable, specialized functions.

heading: Higher Order Functions in JavaScript
text: A higher order function is a function that does at least one of the following: Takes one or more functions as arguments. Returns a function as its result. This works because functions in JavaScript are first-class values.

heading: Taking a Function as an Argument
text: function repeat(times, action) { for (let i = 0; i < times; i++) { action(i); } } repeat(3, (i) => console.log(`Run ${i}`));

heading: Returning a Function
text: function multiplier(factor) { return (number) => number * factor; } const double = multiplier(2); double(5); // 10

heading: map()
text: Transforms each element and returns a new array. [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2); // [2, 4, 6]

heading: filter()
text: Returns a new array with elements that pass a test. [1, 2, 3, 4].filter(n => n % 2 === 0); // [2, 4]

heading: reduce()
text: Reduces an array to a single value. [1, 2, 3, 4].reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 10

heading: forEach()
text: Runs a function for each element. [1, 2, 3].forEach(n => console.log(n));

heading: sort()
text: Sorts using a compare function. [3, 1, 2].sort((a, b) => a - b); // [1, 2, 3]

heading: Chaining
text: const total = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] .filter(n => n % 2 !== 0) .map(n => n * 10) .reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); console.log(total); // 90

heading: Custom Higher Order Function
text: function applyOperation(a, b, operation) { return operation(a, b); } applyOperation(4, 2, (x, y) => x + y); // 6 applyOperation(4, 2, (x, y) => x * y); // 8

heading: Function Wrapper
text: function withLogging(fn) { return function (...args) { console.log("Calling with", args); const result = fn(...args); console.log("Result:", result); return result; }; } const add = (a, b) => a + b; const loggedAdd = withLogging(add); loggedAdd(2, 3);

heading: Key Points
text: A higher order function accepts and/or returns functions. Array methods like map, filter, and reduce are common examples. They make code shorter, reusable, and more declarative.

heading: Local Storage & Session Storage in JavaScript
text: localStorage and sessionStorage are Web Storage APIs that store key-value pairs in the browser. Keys and values are always stored as strings.

heading: Differences
text: Feature localStorage sessionStorage --- --- --- Lifetime Stays until manually cleared Cleared when the tab is closed Scope Shared across all tabs of the same origin Limited to a single tab Capacity About 5 MB About 5 MB Sent to server No No

heading: Methods
text: Both share the same API. localStorage.setItem("name", "Sam"); // save localStorage.getItem("name"); // "Sam" localStorage.removeItem("name"); // remove one item localStorage.clear(); // remove everything localStorage.length; // number of items localStorage.key(0); // key at index 0 sessionStorage.setItem("token", "abc123"); sessionStorage.getItem("token"); // "abc123"

heading: Shorthand Access
text: localStorage.theme = "dark"; console.log(localStorage.theme); // "dark"

heading: Missing Keys
text: localStorage.getItem("unknown"); // null

heading: Storing Objects and Arrays
text: Values are converted to strings, so use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse. const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25 }; localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify(user)); const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user")); console.log(saved.name); // "Sam" Without JSON.stringify: localStorage.setItem("user", user); localStorage.getItem("user"); // "[object Object]"

heading: Looping Through Items
text: for (let i = 0; i < localStorage.length; i++) { const key = localStorage.key(i); console.log(key, localStorage.getItem(key)); }

heading: Storage Event
text: Fires in other tabs of the same origin when localStorage changes. window.addEventListener("storage", (event) => { console.log(event.key, event.oldValue, event.newValue); });

heading: Common Use Cases
text: localStorage: theme preference, saved settings, cached data. sessionStorage: form data for the current tab, temporary state.

heading: Key Points
text: Data is stored as strings only. Data is scoped to the origin (protocol, domain, and port). Do not store sensitive data such as passwords, since the storage is readable by any script on the page.

heading: Nullish Coalescing in JavaScript
text: The nullish coalescing operator (??) returns the right-hand value only when the left-hand value is null or undefined. Otherwise, it returns the left-hand value.

heading: Syntax
text: const result = value ?? defaultValue;

heading: Basic Example
text: null ?? "default"; // "default" undefined ?? "default"; // "default" "hello" ?? "default"; // "hello"

heading: Difference from ||
text: The operator falls back for any falsy value. The ?? operator falls back only for null and undefined. 0 || 10; // 10 0 ?? 10; // 0 "" || "text"; // "text" "" ?? "text"; // "" false || true; // true false ?? true; // false NaN || 5; // 5 NaN ?? 5; // NaN

heading: Practical Example
text: function setVolume(volume) { const level = volume ?? 50; console.log(level); } setVolume(0); // 0 setVolume(undefined); // 50 setVolume(null); // 50

heading: Nullish Assignment (??=)
text: Assigns a value only if the variable is null or undefined. let user = { name: "Sam", age: null }; user.age ??= 18; user.name ??= "Guest"; console.log(user); // { name: "Sam", age: 18 }

heading: Chaining
text: const name = null ?? undefined ?? "Guest"; // "Guest"

heading: Mixing with || and &&
text: ?? cannot be combined directly with or && without parentheses. const a = null || undefined ?? "x"; // SyntaxError const b = (null || undefined) ?? "x"; // "x"

heading: Key Points
text: ?? treats only null and undefined as missing values. Use it when 0, "", and false are valid values. ??= assigns a default only when the value is null or undefined.

topic: Object Oriented JS › ES6 Classes & Inheritance

text: class User { constructor(name, age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } greet() { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; } } const user = new User("Sam", 25); user.greet(); // "Hi, I'm Sam" constructor runs when a new instance is created. Methods are placed on the class's prototype and shared by all instances. A class must be called with new.

text: class Circle { constructor(radius) { this._radius = radius; } get area() { return Math.PI * this._radius ** 2; } set radius(value) { if (value <= 0) throw new Error("Invalid radius"); this._radius = value; } } const c = new Circle(5); c.area; // 78.53... c.radius = 10;

heading: Object Destructuring in JavaScript
text: Object destructuring extracts properties from an object into separate variables using a concise syntax.

heading: Basic Syntax
text: const user = { name: "Sam", age: 25, city: "Ahmedabad" }; const { name, age } = user; console.log(name); // "Sam" console.log(age); // 25 Variable names must match the property names.

heading: Renaming Variables
text: const { name: userName, age: userAge } = user; console.log(userName); // "Sam" console.log(userAge); // 25

heading: Default Values
text: Used when the property is undefined. const { name, country = "India" } = user; console.log(country); // "India"

heading: Renaming with Defaults
text: const { country: userCountry = "India" } = user;

heading: Rest Operator
text: Collects the remaining properties into a new object. const { name, ...others } = user; console.log(name); // "Sam" console.log(others); // { age: 25, city: "Ahmedabad" }

heading: Nested Destructuring
text: const employee = { id: 1, profile: { firstName: "Sam", address: { city: "Ahmedabad", pin: "380001" }, }, }; const { profile: { firstName, address: { city }, }, } = employee; console.log(firstName); // "Sam" console.log(city); // "Ahmedabad" Note: profile and address themselves are not created as variables here.

heading: Destructuring in Function Parameters
text: function greet({ name, age }) { return `${name} is ${age} years old`; } greet(user); // "Sam is 25 years old"

heading: With Defaults
text: function createUser({ name = "Guest", role = "user" } = {}) { return { name, role }; } createUser(); // { name: "Guest", role: "user" } createUser({ name: "Sam" }); // { name: "Sam", role: "user" }

heading: Assigning to Existing Variables

heading: Destructuring in Loops
text: const users = [ { name: "Sam", age: 25 }, { name: "Alex", age: 30 }, ]; for (const { name, age } of users) { console.log(name, age); }

heading: Swapping with Destructuring

heading: Missing Properties
text: const { phone } = user; console.log(phone); // undefined

heading: Destructuring null or undefined
text: const { name } = null; // TypeError Use a fallback to avoid the error. const { name } = maybeUser ?? {};

heading: Key Points
text: Syntax: const { prop1, prop2 } = object. Rename with prop: newName and set defaults with prop = value. Use ...rest to collect the remaining properties. It cannot destructure null or undefined.

heading: Constructor Functions
text: A constructor function is a regular function used with the new keyword to create multiple objects with the same structure. By convention, its name starts with a capital letter. function User(name, age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; this.greet = function () { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; }; } const user1 = new User("Sam", 25); const user2 = new User("Alex", 30); user1.greet(); // "Hi, I'm Sam"

topic: Object Oriented JS › Object literal, Constructors
heading: What new Does
text: Creates a new empty object. Sets the object's prototype to the constructor's prototype. Runs the constructor with this bound to the new object. Returns the object (unless the constructor returns another object).
