text: Routing in Node.js allows you to define how the server responds to various HTTP requests. Advanced routing techniques can be used to create dynamic and flexible routes by using special characters like +, ?, , and regular expressions.

heading: 1. + (Plus)
text: The + character matches one or more occurrences of the preceding character. Example: app.get('/ab+c', (req, res) => { res.send('Route matched: /ab+c'); }); The route /ab+c would match: /abc /abbc /abbbc, and so on.

heading: ? (Question Mark)
text: The ? character makes the preceding character optional in an Express route pattern. Example: app.get('/ab?c', (req, res) => { res.send('Route matched: /ab?c'); }); This route will match: /abc /ac (since b is optional).

heading: (Asterisk)
text: The character matches any sequence of characters in an Express route. Example: app.get('/a*cd', (req, res) => { res.send('Route matched: /a*cd'); }); This route will match: /acd /abcd /axyzcd, etc.

heading: Regular Expressions
text: Regular expressions (regex) can be used in Express routing to match complex patterns. Examples: app.get(/a/, (req, res) => { res.send('Route matched any path containing "a"'); }); This route will match: /abc /a123 /123a, etc.

heading: Understanding NPM
text: A practical, SDE-1-level guide to npm (Node Package Manager), covering how npm works, how to manage dependencies, how packages are resolved and executed, how to publish packages, and how to troubleshoot real-world Node.js projects. What is npm? npm originally stood for Node Package Manager. It is the default package manager for Node.js and consists broadly of: A CLI used from the terminal. A registry where packages are published and downloaded. A package/dependency resolution system. A package metadata and versioning ecosystem. npm allows developers to: Install third-party libraries. Install development tools. Manage project dependencies. Run project scripts. Publish reusable packages. Share code across projects. Reproduce dependency installations across machines and CI environments. Example: npm install express This generally: Resolves the requested package and its dependencies. Downloads the required package metadata/artifacts. Places packages under node_modules. Updates package.json. Updates package-lock.json. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Node.js, npm, and npx
text: These three are related but serve different purposes. Node.js Node.js is the JavaScript runtime. node app.js runs JavaScript using Node.js. npm npm manages packages and project dependencies. npm install express npx npx executes package binaries. For example: npx eslint . You can think of them as: Node.js -> Runs JavaScript npm -> Installs/manages packages npx -> Executes package-provided CLI binaries Modern npm distributions include npx. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Installing and Verifying npm
text: Installing Node.js normally installs npm as well. Check versions: node -v npm -v npx -v Useful diagnostic command: npm doctor The exact output depends on the installed Node.js/npm versions and operating system. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Registry
text: The npm registry is the package repository used by npm. The default public registry is: https://registry.npmjs.org/ A package can contain: Package name Version Description Dependencies Entry points README License Repository metadata Published files Search packages: npm search express View package metadata: npm view express View a specific field: npm view express version npm view express dependencies npm view express dist.tarball ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: package.json
text: package.json is one of the most important files in a Node.js project. Create one: npm init or: npm init -y A basic example: { "name": "my-app", "version": "1.0.0", "description": "Example Node.js application", "main": "index.js", "scripts": { "start": "node index.js", "dev": "node --watch index.js", "test": "node --test" }, "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" }, "devDependencies": { "eslint": "^9.0.0" }, "engines": { "node": ">=20" }, "license": "MIT" } Important package.json fields name Package/project name. "name": "my-app" For published packages, the name must follow npm naming rules. version The package's current version. "version": "1.0.0" description Short description of the package. main Historically used as the CommonJS entry point. "main": "index.js" For modern packages, exports is often preferred. type Controls how .js files are interpreted. "type": "module" means .js files are treated as ES modules. Without it, .js files are generally treated as CommonJS unless another rule applies. scripts Defines commands that can be run using npm. "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch src/index.js", "start": "node src/index.js" } Run: npm run dev npm start dependencies Packages required by the application at runtime. "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" } devDependencies Packages required primarily for development, testing, linting, building, etc. "devDependencies": { "eslint": "^9.0.0" } peerDependencies Used when the package expects the consuming project to provide a compatible dependency. Common in: React libraries UI component libraries Plugins Framework integrations Example: "peerDependencies": { "react": ">=18" } optionalDependencies Dependencies that are allowed to fail during installation without necessarily failing the entire installation. bundledDependencies Dependencies that are included inside the published package. Use this only when there is a concrete reason; ordinary dependencies are normally preferable. engines Specifies supported runtime versions. "engines": { "node": ">=20" } This communicates compatibility expectations but should not be treated as a substitute for runtime enforcement. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: package-lock.json
text: package-lock.json records the dependency tree resolved for a project. It helps provide: Reproducible installations. Exact package versions. Integrity information. Dependency relationships. Faster and more deterministic CI installations. A simplified relationship is: package.json | | declares acceptable versions v package-lock.json | | records resolved versions v node_modules | | contains installed packages Should package-lock.json be committed? For applications, generally yes. Commit: package.json package-lock.json Do not normally commit: node_modules/ ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: node_modules
text: node_modules contains installed dependencies. Example: project/ ├── node_modules/ ├── src/ ├── package.json └── package-lock.json You normally should not manually edit files inside node_modules. If dependencies become corrupted, a common clean reinstall is: rm -rf node_modules npm ci On Windows PowerShell, an equivalent approach is: Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules npm ci ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Dependencies vs Dev Dependencies vs Peer Dependencies
text: This distinction is important in professional development. dependencies Required for the application to run. Example: "dependencies": { "express": "^5.1.0" } devDependencies Required for development/build/test workflows. Example: "devDependencies": { "typescript": "^5.0.0", "eslint": "^9.0.0" } peerDependencies Used by libraries when the host application is expected to provide a dependency. Example: "peerDependencies": { "react": ">=18" } Rule of thumb Ask: "Does the production application need this package to execute?" If yes, it is generally a dependency. If it is only required to build, test, lint, format, or develop the project, it is generally a devDependency. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Semantic Versioning
text: npm packages commonly use Semantic Versioning (SemVer). Format: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH Example: 2.4.7 means: 2 -\> MAJOR 4 -\> MINOR 7 -\> PATCH MAJOR Breaking API changes. 2.x.x -> 3.x.x MINOR Backward-compatible features. 2.4.x -> 2.5.x PATCH Backward-compatible bug fixes. 2.4.7 -> 2.4.8 Pre-release versions can look like: 2.5.0-beta.1 ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Version Ranges
text: npm supports version ranges. Exact version "express": "5.1.0" Only that version is requested. Caret "express": "^5.1.0" Generally permits compatible updates that do not change the left-most non-zero major/minor compatibility boundary. For a normal major version: ^5.1.0 allows versions: >=5.1.0 <6.0.0 Tilde "express": "~5.1.0" Generally allows patch-level updates: >=5.1.0 <5.2.0 Wildcards "express": "5.x" or: "express": "*" Avoid overly broad ranges unless there is a specific reason. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Installing Packages
text: Install a production dependency npm install express Shortcut: npm i express Install a development dependency npm install --save-dev eslint Shortcut: npm i -D eslint Install a specific version npm install express@5.1.0 Install the latest version npm install express@latest Install a package globally npm install -g typescript Use global installation mainly for tools that you intentionally want available system-wide. Project dependencies should normally be local. Install all project dependencies npm install npm reads package.json and the lockfile when available. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Removing and Updating Packages
text: Remove: npm uninstall express Update packages within their declared ranges: npm update Check outdated dependencies: npm outdated View installed dependency tree: npm ls View a specific package: npm ls express ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Scripts
text: Scripts are commands defined in package.json. Example: { "scripts": { "dev": "node --watch src/server.js", "start": "node src/server.js", "lint": "eslint .", "test": "node --test" } } Run: npm run dev npm start npm run lint npm test Some scripts have special shorthand: npm start npm test npm restart npm stop Why scripts matter They standardize project commands. Instead of asking every developer to remember: node --watch src/server.js the project can provide: npm run dev This becomes particularly valuable in teams and CI/CD pipelines. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npx
text: npx runs executables supplied by npm packages. Example: npx eslint . For a package that exposes a CLI: npx <package-command> A useful mental model: npm install -> acquire/manage packages npx -> execute package binaries For reproducible project tooling, prefer using the project's locally installed version rather than relying on an unrelated global installation. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Global vs Local Packages
text: Local installation npm install eslint --save-dev The package is available to the project. Typical location: node_modules/.bin/ npm scripts automatically make local binaries available on PATH. Global installation npm install -g eslint The package is installed into npm's global prefix. Check the global prefix: npm prefix -g Best practice For project-specific tooling: Prefer local installation. This avoids "works on my machine" problems caused by different global versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: How npm Resolves Dependencies
text: Suppose your application depends on: A and A depends on: B The resulting graph is: Application └── A └── B Now suppose another package also requires B: Application ├── A │ └── B └── C └── B npm tries to construct a valid dependency tree while avoiding unnecessary duplication. The exact tree depends on: Requested version ranges. npm version. Peer dependencies. Existing lockfile. Platform. Optional dependencies. Package metadata. Understanding npm as a dependency graph resolver, rather than merely a downloader, is important for debugging. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm install vs npm ci
text: This is a very common SDE-1 and production question. npm install Used for normal development. npm install It can: Resolve dependencies. Update the lockfile when necessary. Install packages. Reconcile package.json and the lockfile. npm ci Primarily intended for clean, automated, reproducible installations. npm ci Important characteristics: Requires a compatible lockfile. Installs from the lockfile. Removes existing node_modules before installation. Does not intentionally update the lockfile. Commonly used in CI/CD. Typical workflow Developer: npm install CI: npm ci ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Dependency Trees and Deduplication
text: Use: npm ls to inspect dependencies. A project can accidentally contain multiple versions of the same package: node_modules/ ├── package-a/ │ └── node_modules/ │ └── lodash@4.x └── lodash@4.x npm can sometimes deduplicate compatible dependencies. Command: npm dedupe However, do not assume every duplicate can or should be removed. Different packages may legitimately require incompatible versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Workspaces
text: Workspaces allow multiple packages to live in one repository. Example: monorepo/ ├── package.json ├── package-lock.json └── packages/ ├── api/ │ └── package.json ├── web/ │ └── package.json └── shared/ └── package.json Root package.json: { "private": true, "workspaces": [ "packages/*" ] } Workspaces are useful for: Monorepos. Shared libraries. Frontend + backend repositories. Internal packages. Shared TypeScript utilities. Example: npm install from the root can install workspace dependencies. Run a workspace script: npm run build --workspace=web Workspaces are different from simply having multiple unrelated Node.js projects in the same Git repository. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: npm Configuration and .npmrc
text: npm configuration can be controlled using: .npmrc Configuration can exist at different levels, including: Project level. User level. Global level. Environment variables / CLI flags. Inspect configuration: npm config list Get a specific value: npm config get registry Set a value: npm config set registry https://registry.npmjs.org/ Important caution Never commit credentials or authentication tokens into .npmrc. For private registries, authentication should be handled securely using environment variables, CI secrets, or supported npm authentication mechanisms. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Environment Variables and Secrets
text: Do not put secrets directly into: package.json .npmrc Git source code Bad: { "someToken": "actual-secret-value" } Prefer environment variables and secret managers. For CI/CD, configure secrets through the CI platform. A common .gitignore includes: node_modules/ .env .env.* Be careful: some projects intentionally commit non-secret .env.example files. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Private Registries and Scoped Packages
text: npm supports scoped packages: @company/package-name Example: npm install @company/shared-utils Organizations can use private registries to distribute internal packages. A project can configure a registry for a scope: @company:registry=https://registry.example.com/ This allows different scopes to resolve through different registries. Private package authentication should be configured securely and never hard-coded into source control. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Publishing an npm Package
text: Before publishing, ensure: { "name": "my-package", "version": "1.0.0" } Login: npm login Inspect what will be published: npm pack --dry-run This is extremely useful because it shows which files will be included. Publish: npm publish For scoped public packages, depending on package configuration: npm publish --access public Versioning before publishing Patch: npm version patch Minor: npm version minor Major: npm version major These commands update the package version and typically create the corresponding Git metadata depending on configuration. Important Do not treat publishing as: write code -> npm publish A professional release process should also consider: Tests. Build output. Package contents. README. License. Versioning. Changelog. Security. Compatibility. Access control. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Package Entry Points and Exports
text: A package needs a clear public API. Historically: { "main": "index.js" } Modern packages can use: { "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js" } } exports provides stronger control over which files consumers can import. Example: { "exports": { ".": "./dist/index.js", "./utils": "./dist/utils.js" } } Then consumers can use: import packageName from "package-name"; or: import { helper } from "package-name/utils"; depending on the package's module format and exports. A key concept: exports defines the package's supported public import surface. This can prevent consumers from depending on internal implementation files. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: CommonJS vs ESM
text: Node.js supports both major JavaScript module systems. CommonJS const express = require("express"); module.exports = myFunction; ES Modules import express from "express"; export default myFunction; A package can declare ESM behavior using: { "type": "module" } CommonJS can explicitly use: .cjs ES modules can explicitly use: .mjs Why SDE-1 developers should understand this Many npm errors are actually module-system errors: require is not defined Cannot use import statement outside a module ERR_REQUIRE_ESM When debugging, inspect: package.json "type" File extensions Package exports Whether the dependency is CommonJS or ESM ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Lifecycle and Pre/Post Scripts
text: npm supports lifecycle scripts. For example: { "scripts": { "prebuild": "npm run clean", "build": "tsc", "postbuild": "node scripts/postbuild.js" } } Running: npm run build can cause: prebuild ↓ build ↓ postbuild There are also lifecycle events associated with installation and publishing. Security consideration Lifecycle scripts can execute code during package installation or other npm operations. This is one reason dependency trust and supply-chain security matter. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Security
text: npm projects are exposed to software supply-chain risks. Major categories include: Malicious packages. Compromised dependencies. Vulnerable dependencies. Typosquatting. Dependency confusion. Malicious install scripts. Credential leakage. Stale dependencies. Untrusted transitive dependencies. Typosquatting An attacker may publish a package with a name similar to a popular package. Example concept: popular-package populer-package Always verify package names before installing. Dependency confusion An internal package name can accidentally resolve to a malicious public package if registry configuration is incorrect. Scoped private packages and explicit registry configuration help reduce this risk. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Auditing and Vulnerability Management
text: Check vulnerabilities: npm audit Attempt automatic fixes: npm audit fix Be careful with aggressive upgrades because security fixes can introduce breaking changes. You should understand: Direct dependency ↓ Transitive dependency ↓ Vulnerable package A vulnerability may exist in a package you never directly installed. Useful commands: npm audit npm ls <package-name> npm explain <package-name> npm explain can help identify why a package exists in the dependency tree. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Reproducible Builds and CI/CD
text: A production Node.js project should aim for reproducible dependency installation. Typical CI flow: Clone repository ↓ Install Node.js ↓ npm ci ↓ Run lint ↓ Run tests ↓ Build ↓ Package/deploy Example: npm ci npm test npm run build The lockfile is important because different developers should not randomly receive different transitive dependency versions. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Caching
text: npm maintains a local cache. Inspect: npm cache verify Clean the cache only when there is a concrete reason: npm cache clean --force Do not make cache deletion your default response to every npm problem. Many npm issues are caused by: Incorrect package versions. Peer dependency conflicts. Broken lockfiles. Registry/authentication issues. Node/npm incompatibility. Platform-specific optional dependencies. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Troubleshooting npm
text: "Module not found" Example: Cannot find module 'express' Check: npm ls express If missing: npm install express Also verify that you are running the command from the correct project directory. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Delete node_modules and reinstall When the dependency installation is genuinely corrupted: rm -rf node_modules npm ci On Windows PowerShell: Remove-Item -Recurse -Force node_modules npm ci ------------------------------------------------------------------------ package-lock.json conflict If package.json and the lockfile are inconsistent, understand why before deleting the lockfile. For a clean CI environment: npm ci requires the lockfile to satisfy npm's expectations. Do not blindly delete package-lock.json as a first troubleshooting step. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Peer dependency conflict You may see errors such as: ERESOLVE unable to resolve dependency tree First understand the conflicting package requirements. Inspect: npm ls npm explain <package> Avoid immediately using: npm install --legacy-peer-deps as a permanent solution. It can bypass dependency resolution protections and leave an invalid or unsupported combination. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ EACCES / permission errors On Unix-like systems, permission errors can happen when npm directories are owned by another user. Investigate: npm config get prefix Avoid solving the problem by routinely running npm with: sudo npm install A correct Node/npm installation and user-level configuration is preferable. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Registry problems Check: npm config get registry Expected public registry: https://registry.npmjs.org/ If using a company registry, verify: Registry URL. Authentication. Scope configuration. Network/VPN. Proxy configuration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Network errors Common errors include: ETIMEDOUT ECONNRESET EAI_AGAIN Possible causes: Internet connectivity. DNS. Proxy. VPN. Corporate firewall. Registry outage. Do not immediately assume the package itself is broken. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ "Works on my machine" Check: node -v npm -v Then compare: Node.js version npm version package.json package-lock.json OS CPU architecture environment variables Use: npm ci in CI to reduce environment-dependent dependency differences. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Performance and Dependency Hygiene
text: A good SDE-1 should not only know how to install packages but also understand the cost of dependencies. Consider: Number of dependencies. Package size. Transitive dependency count. Startup overhead. Security exposure. Maintenance status. License compatibility. Runtime vs build-time usage. Before adding a dependency, ask: Do I really need it? Is the package maintained? Is the API stable? Is it secure? Is the package size reasonable? Can the functionality be implemented safely without another dependency? Do not add a large library for a trivial utility unless the trade-off makes sense. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Useful npm Commands
text: Project initialization npm init npm init -y Installation npm install npm install <package> npm install <package>@<version> npm install -D <package> npm install -g <package> Removal npm uninstall <package> Updates npm update npm outdated npm install <package>@latest Inspection npm ls npm ls <package> npm explain <package> npm view <package> npm config list npm config get registry Scripts npm run <script> npm start npm test Security npm audit npm audit fix Cache npm cache verify npm cache clean --force Package publishing npm login npm pack --dry-run npm publish Versioning npm version patch npm version minor npm version major Dependency graph npm ls npm explain <package> npm dedupe

heading: Practical Checklist
text: Before considering your npm fundamentals SDE-1 ready, you should be comfortable with: Package Management [ ] npm init [ ] npm install [ ] npm uninstall [ ] npm update [ ] npm outdated [ ] npm ls [ ] npm explain Dependency Management [ ] dependencies [ ] devDependencies [ ] peerDependencies [ ] optionalDependencies [ ] Transitive dependencies [ ] Dependency trees [ ] Deduplication Versioning [ ] SemVer [ ] Major/minor/patch [ ] Caret ranges [ ] Tilde ranges [ ] Exact versions [ ] Lockfiles Project Configuration [ ] package.json [ ] package-lock.json [ ] .npmrc [ ] npm scripts [ ] Workspaces [ ] Environment variables Node.js Integration [ ] CommonJS [ ] ESM [ ] type [ ] main [ ] exports [ ] Local binaries [ ] npx Production [ ] npm ci [ ] CI/CD dependency installation [ ] Reproducible builds [ ] Dependency auditing [ ] Security practices [ ] Registry configuration Publishing [ ] npm login [ ] Package naming [ ] Semantic versioning [ ] npm pack --dry-run [ ] npm publish [ ] Package entry points [ ] Public vs private packages ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Mental Model
text: The most useful way to understand npm is to separate its responsibilities: ┌─────────────────────┐ │ npm Registry │ │ Packages + Metadata │ └──────────┬──────────┘ │ │ resolve/download ▼ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ │ package.json │────▶│ npm Resolver │ │ Desired ranges │ │ Dependency │ └──────────────────┘ │ graph │ └───────┬───────┘ │ │ lock exact resolution ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ package-lock │ │ reproducible │ │ resolution │ └───────┬───────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ │ node_modules │ │ Installed │ │ dependency │ │ tree │ └───────────────┘ If you understand this model, most npm behavior becomes easier to reason about. ------------------------------------------------------------------------

heading: Final Takeaway
text: For an SDE-1, npm knowledge is not about memorizing commands. You should understand the system behind the commands: package.json ↓ version ranges ↓ dependency resolution ↓ package-lock.json ↓ node_modules ↓ local binaries / npm scripts ↓ application runtime Then add the production concerns: Security + Reproducibility + CI/CD + Dependency hygiene + Registry management + Versioning + Publishing A developer who understands these concepts can: Set up Node.js projects correctly. Add and remove dependencies safely. Diagnose dependency conflicts. Understand lockfiles. Build reproducible CI/CD pipelines. Identify npm security risks. Publish packages correctly. Work effectively with monorepos and private registries. Debug most common npm-related problems independently. That is the practical npm foundation expected from an SDE-1 working with Node.js-based applications.

AGGREGATE FUNCTIONS The five most used SQL aggregate functions are COUNT(), SUM(), AVG(), MIN(), and MAX(). General Syntax Structure Aggregate functions are generally placed in the SELECT list and are frequently paired with a GROUP BY clause to summarize categories. SELECT column\_name, AGGREGATE\_FUNCTION(column\_to\_aggregate)   FROM table\_name   WHERE condition   GROUP BY column\_name   HAVING AGGREGATE\_FUNCTION(column\_to\_aggregate) > value; General-Purpose Aggregates COUNT(\): Counts total input rows. COUNT(expression): Counts rows with non-null values. SUM(expression): Calculates the total of numeric values. AVG(expression): Computes the arithmetic mean. MIN(expression): Finds the minimum value. MAX(expression): Finds the maximum value. ARRAY\_AGG(expression): Concatenates input values into an array. STRING\_AGG(expression, delimiter): Concatenates values into a single string. JSON\_AGG(expression): Aggregates rows into a JSON array. JSONB\_AGG(expression): Aggregates rows into a JSONB array. JSON\_OBJECT\_AGG(key, value): Aggregates key-value pairs into a JSON object. JSONB\_OBJECT\_AGG(key, value): Aggregates key-value pairs into a JSONB object. BOOL\_AND(expression): Returns true if all values are true. BOOL\_OR(expression): Returns true if any value is true. EVERY(expression): Identical equivalent to BOOL\_AND. XMLAGG(expression): Concatenates XML values across input rows. Statistical Aggregates STDDEV(expression): Alias for sample standard deviation. STDDEV\_SAMP(expression): Computes sample standard deviation. STDDEV\_POP(expression): Computes population standard deviation. VARIANCE(expression): Alias for sample variance. VAR\_SAMP(expression): Computes sample variance. VAR\_POP(expression): Computes population variance. CORR(Y, X): Computes the correlation coefficient. COVAR\_POP(Y, X): Computes population covariance. COVAR\_SAMP(Y, X): Computes sample covariance. Linear Regression Aggregates REGR\_COUNT(Y, X): Counts rows where both inputs are non-null. REGR\_AVGX(Y, X): Computes independent variable average. REGR\_AVGY(Y, X): Computes dependent variable average. REGR\_SLOPE(Y, X): Computes the least-squares-fit slope. REGR\_INTERCEPT(Y, X): Computes the y-intercept value. REGR\_R2(Y, X): Computes the square of correlation coefficient. REGR\_SXX(Y, X): Computes independent "sum of squares". REGR\_SYY(Y, X): Computes dependent "sum of squares". REGR\_SXY(Y, X): Computes "sum of products".

The EXTRACT() function retrieves specific subfields (like year, month, day, hour, or minute) from a date, time, timestamp, or interval value. It returns a value of type numeric (or double precision in older versions) Common Field Subfields YEAR: The full calendar year. QUARTER: The quarter of the year (1 to 4). MONTH: The month number (1 to 12). DAY: The day of the month (1 to 31). DOW: The day of the week (0 = Sunday, 1 = Monday, ..., 6 = Saturday). ISODOW: The ISO 8601 day of the week (1 = Monday, ..., 7 = Sunday). DOY: The day of the year (1 to 365/366). HOUR: The hour component (0 to 23). MINUTE: The minute component (0 to 59). SECOND: The seconds component, including fractional seconds. EPOCH: The total number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC. Examples: SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_year,   EXTRACT(MONTH FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_month,   EXTRACT(DAY FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-07-18 14:30:15') AS order\_day; SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM CURRENT\_TIMESTAMP) AS current\_hour; SELECT \   FROM transactions   WHERE EXTRACT(MONTH FROM transaction\_date) = 5; 2. The CASE expression function acts like an if-then-else statement to add conditional logic directly inside your SQL queries. It runs through conditions in order and returns a value as soon as the first condition is met. Example-1: SELECT   product\_name,   price,   CASE   WHEN price < 10 THEN 'Budget'   WHEN price BETWEEN 10 AND 50 THEN 'Normal'   ELSE 'Premium'   END AS price\_category FROM products; Example-2: SELECT   employee\_name,   department\_id,   CASE department\_id   WHEN 1 THEN 'Engineering'   WHEN 2 THEN 'Marketing'   WHEN 3 THEN 'Sales'   ELSE 'Other'   END AS department\_name FROM employees; Advanced Placement: You are not limited to using CASE in SELECT lists. You can place it inside other clauses. You can embed a CASE expression in almost any statement or clause that accepts a value, column name, or logic check. SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, HAVING, JOIN (specifically ON) Clauses, SET Clause (in UPDATE Statements, VALUES Clause (in INSERT Statements),Nested inside another CASE Expression.

GENERATE\_SERIES() generate\_series() is a built-in Set Returning Function (SRF) used to create ordered lists of numbers, dates, or timestamps on the fly. It behaves like a virtual table, making it highly effective for generating test data, filling missing gaps in reporting timelines, or replacing programmatic loops. Syntax Overview: generate\_series(start, stop \[, step]) start: The beginning value of your sequence. stop: The termination limit; the sequence will not cross this value. step: (Optional) The increment/decrement size. Defaults to 1 for numeric data types. Basic Examples: Generating Numbers: You can generate a sequential list of integers, bigints, or numeric fractions. Default step (1): SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(1, 5); -- Returns: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 Custom step: SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(10, 50, 10); -- Returns: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 Counting backwards (Requires a negative step): SELECT \ FROM generate\_series(5, 1, -1); -- Returns: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1   2. Generating Dates \& Timestamps: When generating time series, the step parameter must be specified as an INTERVAL. Daily interval: SELECT generate\_series(   '2026-07-01'::timestamp,   '2026-07-05'::timestamp,   '1 day'::interval   ) AS days; Hourly interval: SELECT generate\_series(   '2026-07-19 00:00'::timestamp,   '2026-07-19 04:00'::timestamp,   '1 hour'::interval   ) AS hours;

Syntax Writing Order: When writing a SELECT statement in ⁠PostgreSQL, clauses must be written in this exact sequence: SELECT column\_list FROM table\_name JOIN other\_table ON condition WHERE row\_filter\_conditions GROUP BY grouping\_columns HAVING group\_filter\_conditions WINDOW window\_name AS (window\_spec) ORDER BY sorting\_columns LIMIT number\_of\_rows OFFSET number\_to\_skip; Clauses Execution Order: STEP CLAUSE PostgreSQL Execution - - - 1. FROM/JOIN Selects the base tables and merges them to create the initial dataset. 2. WHERE Filters out rows that do not meet individual conditions. 3. GROUP BY Collapses the remaining individual rows into groups. 4. HAVING Filters out aggregated groups that do not meet specified criteria. 5. WINDOW Executes window functions (like ROW\_NUMBER()) over the grouped data. 6. SELECT Emits the final columns and evaluates expressions or structural aliases. 7. DISTINCT Scans the columns to eliminate any duplicate result rows. 8. ORDER BY Sorts the final result set in ascending or descending order. 9. LIMIT/OFFSET Trims the result set to skip a specific number of rows or keep only the top rows. Alias Visibility: Because SELECT runs after WHERE and GROUP BY, you cannot use column aliases inside those clauses. For example, SELECT price \ 2 AS double\_price ... WHERE double\_price > 10 will throw an error. ORDER BY Capabilities: Because ORDER BY executes after SELECT, you can use your SELECT aliases or positional numbers (like ORDER BY 1) to sort your data. WHERE vs. HAVING: Use WHERE to filter raw rows before aggregation, and use HAVING only to filter aggregated values (like COUNT(\) or SUM()).

ROLLUP is a subclause of the GROUP BY clause that allows you to calculate multiple levels of subtotals and a grand total within a single query. It generates hierarchical grouping sets based on the order of the columns provided, reducing the columns from right to left. How ROLLUP Works: When you pass columns to ROLLUP(c1, c2, c3), PostgreSQL assumes a hierarchy where c1 > c2 > c3. It will automatically compute aggregates for the following combinations: (c1, c2, c3) — Detailed group totals. (c1, c2) — Subtotals for each combination of c1 and c2. (c1) — Subtotals for each c1. () — Grand total across the entire table. Basic Syntax: SELECT column1, column2, SUM(column3)   FROM table\_name   GROUP BY ROLLUP (column1, column2); Examples: 1. Consider a sales table containing regional sales data:   region category amount - - - North Electronics 1000 North Electronics 500 South Furniture 1500   SELECT region, category, SUM(amount) AS total\_sales   FROM sales   GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, category)   ORDER BY region, category; Expected Output: region category total\_sales Explanation - - - - North Electronics 1000 Normal Group North Furniture 500 Normal Group North NULL 1500 North Region Subtotal South Electronics 1500 Normal Group South NULL 1500 South Region Subtotal NULL NULL 3000 Grand Total Differentiating NULLs with GROUPING(): When using ROLLUP, rows containing subtotals output a NULL for the columns that have been rolled up. To avoid confusion between a natural NULL in your data and a NULL generated by ROLLUP, you can use the GROUPING() function: SELECT   CASE WHEN GROUPING(region) = 1 THEN 'All Regions' ELSE region END as region,   CASE WHEN GROUPING(category) = 1 THEN 'All Categories' ELSE category END as category,   SUM(amount) AS total\_sales   FROM sales   GROUP BY ROLLUP (region, category); Partial ROLLUP: If you want a grand total and specific subtotals but don't want to roll up every single column, you can leave columns outside the ROLLUP function: GROUP BY region, ROLLUP(category); -- This skips the individual category breakdown subtotals

1\. TO\_CHAR() converts data types like dates, timestamps, or numbers into formatted text strings. The TO\_CHAR() function formats timestamp, interval, integer, float, or numeric data into structured text based on a template. Syntax: TO\_CHAR(value, 'format\_pattern') Common Examples Format Current Date: Formats a date into a standard YYYY-MM-DD layout. SELECT TO\_CHAR(CURRENT\_DATE, 'YYYY-MM-DD'); -- Result: '2026-07-19' Format Time with AM/PM: Extracts 12-hour formatted time with minutes and indicators. SELECT TO\_CHAR(NOW(), 'HH12:MI AM'); -- Result: '05:29 PM' Format Currency \& Decimals: Rounds numbers and maps local currency or thousands separators. SELECT TO\_CHAR(12345.67, '$99,999.99'); -- Result: ' $12,345.67' 2\. The TRIM() Function The TRIM() function strips blank spaces or designated unwanted characters from the edges of text strings. Syntax: TRIM(\[LEADING TRAILING BOTH] \[characters] FROM string) Note: If no positioning or character targets are passed, it defaults to stripping spaces from BOTH ends. Common Examples: Remove Surrounding Spaces: Cleans white space off both sides. SELECT TRIM(' hello world '); -- Result: 'hello world' Remove Leading Characters Only: Strips target elements from the start. SELECT TRIM(LEADING '0' FROM '00012345'); -- Result: '12345' Remove Specific Multi-Character Sets: Strips any matching character from the edge sets. SELECT TRIM(BOTH 'xyz' FROM 'xyxTomxx'); -- Result: 'Tom'

WINDOW Functions PostgreSQL window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them into a single output row. The basic syntax requires an OVER clause, which controls how rows are grouped (PARTITION BY) and sorted (ORDER BY): SELECT column, function() OVER (PARTITION BY group\_col ORDER BY sort\_col) FROM table; Ranking Functions: These functions assign numerical rankings or sequential positions to rows within a partition. ROW\_NUMBER(): Assigns a unique sequential integer to each row starting at 1. RANK(): Assigns rankings with gaps for duplicate values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE\_RANK(): Assigns rankings without any gaps for duplicate values (e.g., 1, 2, 2, 3). PERCENT\_RANK(): Calculates the relative rank of a row as a percentage between 0 and 1. CUME\_DIST(): Calculates the cumulative distribution of a value (relative position) within the partition. NTILE(num\_buckets): Splits rows into a specific number of approximately equal buckets and assigns a bucket ID. Value \& Offset Functions: These functions allow you to grab values from other rows without performing complex self-joins. LAG(col, offset, default): Fetches data from a previous row at a specific offset. LEAD(col, offset, default): Fetches data from a subsequent row at a specific offset. FIRST\_VALUE(col): Returns the value from the very first row in the window frame. LAST\_VALUE(col): Returns the value from the very last row in the window frame. NTH\_VALUE(col, n): Returns the value from the exact n-th row in the window frame. Aggregate Functions (Used as Window Functions): Standard aggregate functions automatically act as window functions when paired with an OVER clause. Instead of a total summary, they produce running calculations. SUM(col): Computes running totals. AVG(col): Computes moving averages. COUNT(col): Computes cumulative counts. MIN(col) / MAX(col): Finds the lowest or highest value in the window.

Hooks let function components use state, side effects, refs, and shared data. ); } Functional updates When the new value depends on the previous one, pass a function. It always receives the latest value. setCount((prev) => prev + 1); Lazy initial state If the initial value is expensive to compute, pass a function. []); Objects and arrays: never mutate, always copy const [user, setUser] = useState({ name: "Asha", age: 24 }); setUser((prev) => ({ ...prev, age: 25 })); // update object const [items, setItems] = useState([]); setItems((prev) => [...prev, "new"]); // add setItems((prev) => prev.filter((i) => i !== "old")); // remove setItems((prev) => prev.map((i) => (i.id === 1 ? { ...i, done: true } : i))); // update Key points The setter replaces state. For objects, spread the old values yourself. Updates are batched and asynchronous: the variable keeps its old value until the next render. Calling the setter with the same value skips the re-render. text: A practical and in-depth reference to Webpack 5: core concepts, configuration, optimization, internals, and interview-ready knowledge. 1\. What is Webpack and Why Use It Webpack is a static module bundler for JavaScript applications. It starts from one or more entry points, builds a dependency graph of every module your project needs (JS, CSS, images, fonts, JSON, WASM, etc.), and emits one or more bundles that browsers (or Node.js) can load. Problems it solves Problem How Webpack helps - - Many tags, order-sensitive, global scope pollution Module system with a single dependency graph; scoped modules Browsers lacking support for newer syntax or module formats Transpilation via loaders (Babel, TypeScript), format interop Non-JS assets (CSS, images, fonts) Treated as modules via loaders / asset modules Large bundles, slow load Code splitting, tree shaking, minification, lazy loading Cache invalidation Content hashing, deterministic IDs, runtime chunk Developer experience Dev server, Hot Module Replacement, source maps Sharing code across apps Module Federation Key characteristics Everything is a module (via loaders / asset modules). Supports ESM, CommonJS, AMD, and mixes of them. Highly configurable and extensible (loaders + plugins + hooks). Built on Tapable, an event/hook system that powers the whole architecture. Has a persistent filesystem cache (v5) for fast rebuilds. 2\. Core Concepts Entry ──► Module graph ──► Loaders transform ──► Chunks ──► Output bundles ▲ ▲ Plugins hook into every stage Concept Purpose - - Entry Where Webpack starts building the dependency graph Output Where and how bundles are emitted Loaders Transform individual files (non-JS to JS, TS to JS, SCSS to CSS) Plugins Extend Webpack across the whole build lifecycle (HTML generation, minification, env injection) Mode development, production, or none; sets built-in optimizations Module Any file Webpack processes Chunk A group of modules bundled together (a unit of splitting) Bundle The final emitted file(s), generally one per chunk Dependency graph The tree/graph of module relationships Runtime / Manifest Small bootstrap code that wires modules and chunks together at runtime \\Module vs Chunk vs Bundle\\: modules are the source units, chunks are logical groupings created during the build, and bundles are the actual files written to disk. \--- 3\. Installation and Quick Start mkdir my-app \&\& cd my-app npm init -y npm install --save-dev webpack webpack-cli webpack-dev-server Project layout: my-app/ ├── src/ │ └── index.js ├── dist/ ├── package.json └── webpack.config.js src/index.js: import { greet } from './greet'; document.body.textContent = greet('Webpack'); webpack.config.js: const path = require('path'); module.exports = { mode: 'development', entry: './src/index.js', output: { filename: 'main.js', path: path.resolve(\_\_dirname, 'dist'), clean: true, }, }; package.json scripts: { "scripts": { "dev": "webpack serve --open", "build": "webpack --mode production", "watch": "webpack --watch" } } Run npm run build; output lands in dist/. Webpack 5 requires Node.js 10.13+ (use a currently supported LTS in practice). \--- 4\. Configuration Basics Webpack config is a JS module that exports an object, an array of objects (multi-compiler), a function, or a Promise. // webpack.config.js module.exports = { mode: 'production', entry: {}, output: {}, module: { rules: \[] }, plugins: \[], resolve: {}, optimization: {}, devServer: {}, devtool: 'source-map', externals: {}, target: 'web', cache: {}, performance: {}, stats: 'errors-warnings', watchOptions: {}, experiments: {}, }; Config formats // 1. Function (receives env and argv) module.exports = (env, argv) => ({ mode: argv.mode, devtool: argv.mode === 'development' ? 'eval-source-map' : false, }); // 2. heading: Yarn: Complete Guide
text: A practical, in-depth reference for the Yarn package manager: what it is, how it works internally, how to use it day to day, how to run it in CI and monorepos, and how it stacks up against npm (with a short note on pnpm). Version note: Yarn's feature set differs significantly between Yarn Classic (1.x) and Yarn Berry (2.x, 3.x, 4.x). Commands and behaviors below are labeled where they differ. Always check the official docs for the release you're using, since details change between minor versions. What Is Yarn? Yarn is a package manager for JavaScript and TypeScript projects. It installs, updates, and removes dependencies declared in package.json, resolves the full dependency tree, records exact resolved versions in a lockfile, and runs project scripts. It is compatible with the npm registry (registry.npmjs.org), so every package published to npm is installable with Yarn. Core promises: Deterministic installs: the same lockfile yields the same dependency tree on every machine. Speed: parallel downloads, a global/offline cache, and (in modern Yarn) installs that skip creating node_modules entirely. Correctness: strict dependency resolution (especially with PnP) that prevents code from importing packages it never declared ("phantom dependencies"). First-class monorepo support through workspaces. --- History and Versions Era Name Version Status --- --- --- --- 2016 Yarn Classic 1.x (latest 1.22.x) Maintenance mode. Receives only critical fixes. 2020 Yarn Berry 2.x Rewrite in TypeScript; introduced PnP by default, plugins, constraints. 2021 Yarn Berry 3.x Performance and ergonomics improvements. 2023+ Yarn Berry 4.x Current line. Requires a modern Node.js (18+). Background: Yarn was created at Facebook (now Meta) with Google, Exponent, and Tilde to fix npm's problems at the time: non-deterministic installs, slow installs, and weak offline support. It pushed npm to adopt lockfiles (npm 5, 2017) and many other improvements. "Berry" is the codename for Yarn 2+. It is a ground-up rewrite, not a drop-in upgrade from 1.x. The yarn binary you invoke is a thin shim that loads the version pinned by the project. Classic and Berry have different configuration files (.yarnrc vs .yarnrc.yml), lockfile formats, and many command names/flags. Rule of thumb: for new projects choose Yarn 4 (Berry) or npm/pnpm. Avoid starting new projects on Yarn 1.x unless a constraint forces it. --- Installation and Version Management Recommended: Corepack Corepack is a tool that manages package manager versions per project. It shipped with Node.js for many releases. Newer Node.js releases (starting with Node 25) no longer bundle it, so you may need to install it yourself. # Install Corepack if your Node.js doesn't bundle it npm install -g corepack # Enable shims for yarn/pnpm corepack enable # Pin Yarn for a project (writes the packageManager field in package.json) corepack use yarn@stable # or a specific version corepack use yarn@4.9.2 Pinning happens through the packageManager field: { "name": "my-app", "packageManager": "yarn@4.9.2" } Anyone running yarn in the project then automatically gets that exact version, with no global install and no version drift between developers and CI. Alternative: yarn set version From within a project (with any Yarn available): yarn set version stable # latest Yarn Berry yarn set version 4.9.2 # specific version yarn set version classic # Yarn 1.x This downloads the release into .yarn/releases/ and records it as yarnPath in .yarnrc.yml. Commit that file so the whole team uses the same version. Other options npm install -g yarn installs Yarn Classic 1.x (not Berry). Fine for bootstrapping; use yarn set version afterward. System packages (Homebrew, apt, Chocolatey) tend to provide Classic and lag behind. Verify yarn --version --- Core Concepts package.json: declares the project, dependencies (dependencies, devDependencies, peerDependencies, optionalDependencies), and scripts. Lockfile (yarn.lock): records the exact resolved version, checksum, and dependency graph. Cache: compressed archives of every package version. In Berry it is a first-class, optionally committed artifact (.yarn/cache). Linker: the strategy for making installed packages available to Node.js (PnP, node_modules, or pnpm-style). Workspaces: multiple packages in one repository sharing one lockfile. Resolution vs. fetch vs. link: Yarn's install is three phases. Resolution computes the dependency graph and updates the lockfile; fetch downloads archives into the cache; link makes packages importable. Descriptors vs. locators: Berry terminology. A descriptor is a request (lodash@^4.17.0); a locator is a concrete resolution (lodash@npm:4.17.21). You'll see both in yarn.lock and error messages. --- Command Cheat Sheet (Yarn vs npm) Everyday commands Task Yarn 4 (Berry) Yarn 1 (Classic) npm --- --- --- --- Install all dependencies yarn / yarn install yarn npm install Reproducible CI install yarn install --immutable yarn install --frozen-lockfile npm ci Add a dependency yarn add pkg yarn add pkg npm install pkg Add a dev dependency yarn add -D pkg yarn add -D pkg npm install -D pkg Add a peer dependency yarn add -P pkg yarn add -P pkg npm install --save-peer pkg Add exact version yarn add -E pkg yarn add -E pkg npm install -E pkg Remove a dependency yarn remove pkg yarn remove pkg npm uninstall pkg Upgrade a package yarn up pkg yarn upgrade pkg npm update pkg Upgrade interactively yarn upgrade-interactive yarn upgrade-interactive (none built-in; use npm-check-updates) Show outdated packages yarn upgrade-interactive (shows outdated) yarn outdated npm outdated Why is X installed? yarn why pkg yarn why pkg npm explain pkg (alias npm why) List installed packages yarn info -R / yarn info --all yarn list npm ls Package info from registry yarn npm info pkg yarn info pkg npm view pkg Deduplicate yarn dedupe (manual / yarn-deduplicate) npm dedupe Run a script yarn run build or yarn build yarn build npm run build Run a binary from deps yarn exec tool / yarn tool yarn tool npm exec tool / npx tool One-off remote package yarn dlx pkg (not available; use npx) npx pkg / npm exec Security audit yarn npm audit yarn audit npm audit Publish yarn npm publish yarn publish npm publish Log in to registry yarn npm login yarn login npm login Clean cache yarn cache clean yarn cache clean npm cache clean --force Get/set config yarn config get/set yarn config get/set npm config get/set Init project yarn init yarn init npm init Rebuild native deps yarn rebuild yarn install --force npm rebuild Print package manager version yarn --version yarn --version npm --version Yarn-specific commands (Berry) Command Purpose --- --- yarn set version Pin the Yarn version for the project yarn plugin import Install a plugin yarn workspaces list List all workspaces yarn workspaces foreach ... Run a command across workspaces yarn workspaces focus Install only the deps needed by given workspaces (great for Docker/CI) yarn patch / yarn patch-commit Patch a dependency in place (built-in patch-package equivalent) yarn unplug Extract a package from the zip cache to disk (PnP) yarn constraints Enforce rules across workspaces yarn explain peer-requirements Debug peer dependency warnings yarn sdks Generate editor SDKs for PnP (VS Code, etc.) yarn node Run Node with the PnP runtime loaded yarn bin Print the path to a binary yarn version Release/versioning workflow for (monorepo) packages Note: In Berry, yarn global was removed. For global-style tools use yarn dlx, or install a tool per project. Classic's yarn global add still exists in 1.x. --- Install Strategies Yarn's nodeLinker setting (in .yarnrc.yml) controls how installed packages are exposed to Node.js: nodeLinker What it does Pros Cons --- --- --- --- pnp (default in Berry) No node_modules. A .pnp.cjs map tells Node where each package lives (usually inside zip archives). Fastest installs, strict correctness, tiny disk footprint, enables zero-installs Tooling compatibility issues, needs editor
